episodes.title: Two Lines
paras: The second line showed up before the buzzer did.

Gigi Gavin sat on the closed lid of a toilet in the staff bathroom under the arena, with the roar of four thousand people coming through the concrete above her and a plastic stick in her hand, and she watched the second line arrive the way you watch weather come in over water. Slowly. Then all at once. Then like it had always been there.
Positive. The box had used a friendlier word, but the box was selling something.

Above her, the conference final was ending. She could feel it in the floor — the whole building leaning one way, the way it leaned when Blake Kreave had the ball and the last minute on the clock. Somewhere up there, past the ceiling and the noise, he was doing the thing he did that made grown men who owned buildings stand up in their seats. Somewhere up there, when it ended, Layna Morris would come over the barrier in her cheer uniform and kiss him in front of the cameras, because that was the photograph the academy sold.
Down here, the help was pregnant.

Gigi counted backward on her fingers, because her phone was in her apron and her hands needed a job. December. The championship. Of course it was the championship — the biggest night of his life, the night he had come down the tunnel afterward still shaking, still lit up like a struck match, and found her in the equipment room stacking towels, and looked at her the way he only ever looked at her, like she was the one room in the building where he was allowed to breathe. Eight weeks. She counted again, slower, like arithmetic might have mercy. Eight weeks.
The buzzer went off through the concrete and the building came apart with joy.

She wrapped the stick in a paper towel, then in another one, buried it in the deep pocket of her laundry cart, and went back to work. That was the rule of her whole life at Bridge Water, and she had learned it before she could drive: whatever is happening to you, the towels still need folding. The kingdom does not pause for the staff.

By the time the team came down the tunnel, she had the cart parked in its alcove and her face set to the expression she wore for all of them — pleasant, invisible, a girl made of helpfulness. The players came through howling, drenched, golden, holding the trophy over their heads like an offering. Franky came first, screaming her name the way he always did, because Franky was the only one of them who had ever learned it. "Gigi! Tell me you saw it. Tell me the laundry saw it."
"The laundry sees everything," she said. "That's the job."

Then Blake came through, last, the way the star always comes last, and the tunnel went tight and bright around him. He had confetti in his hair. He had the game on his skin like a second, better shirt. Layna was still up in the lights where she belonged, being photographed being his, and he was down here, being pulled apart by teammates, and in the middle of all of it — in the middle of the noise and the hands and the glory — his eyes found Gigi in her alcove like the building had exactly one door in it.
It lasted one second. It was the most honest second of his whole public life, and she was the only one who saw it.

That was their whole arrangement, written in one look. Everybody at Bridge Water got Blake Kreave in the light. Gigi Gavin got him at two in the morning, in the equipment room, smelling of bleach and other people's victories, with his guard so far down it was in another state. She had never once confused the two arrangements. She was not confused now. She was just standing in a tunnel with his child folded into a paper towel in her cart, learning that an arrangement can hold for five months and break in one evening without a single word of it changing.
She had met him in September, in this same tunnel, in the second week of the season. Not met — found. There is a difference, and the difference is the whole story.

He had come off the field at halftime white as paper, and while the team went up the ramp screaming, he had peeled off into the service corridor and been sick behind the equipment cages with a precision that told her he had done it before and planned the location. She had been mending a torn warm-up jacket. She had watched the kingdom's golden boy brace himself against the cage with both hands, shaking, and she had said the first true thing anyone had ever said to him at this school.
"You don't look like a king right now."
He had laughed, because there was nothing else to do with it. "Don't tell."
"I never tell," she had said. "That's the job."

He had looked at her then — really looked, the way he had looked at her tonight — and she had understood, standing there with a needle in her hand, that the most famous boy at Bridge Water was a hostage with excellent cheekbones, and that she had just become the keeper of the only secret he had. It took him three weeks to come back to the corridor on purpose. It took him one more to admit, at two in the morning, surrounded by other people's laundry, that the corridor was the only place in the building where his chest didn't hurt.

What he had, that first month, was information he had never given anyone: that his father timed his phone calls to the minute and opened every one with the score; that his mother kept a seating chart for his life the way she kept one for her galas, and Layna Morris had been seated beside him in both since they were twelve; that being Blake Kreave was a job with a uniform and a crowd and no clock-out, and the corridor — bleach, steam, a scholarship girl with a needle — was the only unpaid hour in his schedule. He kept arriving with two coffees and a terror of being ordinary, and she kept being the only person alive who didn't want anything from him, which in his world made her either a saint or a bomb. It turned out she was both. It just took until February for the bomb part to get its paperwork in order.
Nobody warned you, Gigi thought now, pushing the cart toward the laundry while the arena emptied its happiness into the night, that the keeper of a man's only secret eventually becomes the secret.

It should also be said — because the academy never said it, which is how she got away with it — that Blake Kreave's secrets were not the first true things Gigi Gavin had kept in the dark. The referee who had ended a senior's season, and a senior's scholarship, with one lazy call in November still told the story of his ruined car like a haunting: four tires, one long night, no witnesses, no cameras, no earthly reason to look at the girl who did the team's laundry. She had never looked back at him either. That was the thing about being invisible, the thing nobody who'd never been it understood: it wasn't only a wound. It was also a weapon. She had been carrying it longer than she had been carrying Blake Kreave's heart, and unlike his heart, it had never once asked her to be gentle. She had held his panic, his terror of his father, his hatred of the announcement calendar, the real laugh he never used in photographs. She had held all of it the way she held everything — quietly, at her own expense, out of sight. And now there was one more thing of his in her keeping, except this one was also hers, and it had a heartbeat, or would soon, and it could not be folded and shelved and pretended out of existence by an act of scheduling.
The laundry was empty except for Misty, who was sitting on the dryer she was not supposed to sit on, eating dining-hall fries out of a cup like the world's smallest queen.

"Kingdom's happy," Misty said. "You missed the king's speech. He thanked the fans, the coaches, and quote, everyone who makes this place run. That's us. We got thanked in a group with the concession stands."
"Frame it," Gigi said. "Put it toward my tuition."
Misty looked at her a moment longer than a joke required. "You look like a ghost at a wedding, Gavin."
"I'm fine."

"You're doing the thing where you fold like the towels owe you money." Misty slid the fries toward her, an offering between broke people, which is to say a sacrament. "Eat. Whatever it is, it's worse on an empty stomach. That's science. I read it on a poster in a clinic once."

Gigi did not eat. The smell of the grease came off the cup and the laundry tilted, gently, like a boat deciding something, and she put one hand flat on the warm dryer and breathed through her mouth and understood that her body had already started telling the truth to people — that it would keep telling it, louder, on a schedule set by no one in this building, least of all her.
"Stomach bug," she said.
"Right," said Misty, who did not believe her and loved her enough to file the disbelief for later. "Eat when the bug allows."
"I look like staff," Gigi said, and fed a load of the kingdom's towels into the wash, and the ordinary mercy of the machines took the conversation away.

The service door sighed once while the machines were running, and Roach came through it the way weather comes through a crack — sideways, unbothered, carrying a gym duffel that was heavier than laundry had any right to be. He set it on her cart without a word. Gigi slid it under the towels bound for the field house without looking inside, because looking inside was not the service she sold. The service she sold was that there was nothing to see: a scholarship girl, a cart, the kingdom's towels, rolling through every checkpoint in the building like furniture.
"You're a lifesaver, Gavin," Roach said.
"I never saw it," Gigi said.
"That's why you're the lifesaver."

Some girls at Bridge Water had allowances. Gigi had credit — with the one economy on campus that never asked for her name, her paperwork, or her story, and whose account book, like hers, existed entirely in memory. She had been washing more than towels since October. It paid in favors, and favors, unlike wages, could be spent in the dark.

episodes.title: Not Yet
paras: Between the laundry and the last of the towels, her route took her past the mouth of the main tunnel, where the victory party was still going on under the bright lights — the team, the squad, the parents with buildings named after them, the boosters with their checkbooks out like songbooks. At the press table at the edge of the light, Priest sat typing with the calm of a man taking dictation at an execution, filing the kingdom's official memory while it was still warm. He did not look up. Priest never looked up; the whole academy confessed itself in his direction eventually, and they both knew she would too, someday, some way. And in the center of the light, on the arm of a laughing boy who had just been handed another piece of his future, stood Layna Morris — damp-haired, radiant, exactly where the seating chart had put her when she was twelve — looking, for one unphotographed instant when she thought the cameras were reloading, as tired as anyone Gigi had ever seen at this school.

Then the cameras came back up, and so did Layna's face, and Gigi pushed her cart into the dark and did the arithmetic of her own life instead, which was simpler: one test, two lines, zero people she could tell.

She worked the rest of the shift the way she had worked every shift since September: expertly, invisibly, with the second line sitting in her stomach like a stone in a coat pocket. She thought about the conduct clause in her scholarship housing agreement, which she had actually read, because poor girls read the paperwork. She thought about the word morality doing its quiet work in paragraph nine. She thought about her mother's voice on the phone saying we are so proud, baby, in a kitchen four hundred miles from the nearest person who knew what pride was costing her daughter. She thought about the clinic across from the academy gates, the one with the door that stayed lit all night like an eye that never judged anybody, and she thought about walking through it, and the thought was so reasonable, so clean, so survivable, that she held it very carefully and did not trust it at all.

At midnight the building was dark and the court was empty, and he came down the tunnel the way he always came, out of the last of the celebration, with his jacket over his shoulders and the trophy already behind him like weather.
"You stayed," he said.
"I work here," Gigi said. "It's my whole personality. Ask anyone. No one can, because no one knows my name, but ask anyway."

He laughed — the real one, the corridor one — and crossed the equipment room and took her face in both hands like it was the trophy, and kissed her with the confetti still in his hair. For exactly one minute, in the bleach-and-steam dark, the arrangement held the way it had held for five months: she was the room he could breathe in, and he was the one person alive who looked at her like she was a person and not a function. She let herself have the whole minute. She had already decided she was going to remember it as the last one.
Then she took the paper towel out of the cart's deep pocket, and unwrapped it, and held out the future on a plastic stick.

She watched him read it. She had imagined this moment on a loop for three hours — during the folding, during the machines, during Misty's fries — and in every version she had imagined his face doing one thing. It did three. First, for one unguarded second, before the script could get to him, Blake Kreave looked happy. It crossed his face like weather over water, real and unphotographable, and she understood that she would be keeping that second with all the other things of his she kept. Then the terror arrived, exactly on schedule, and started doing arithmetic on his features. Then — and this was the part that would stay with her longer than either — he got gentle. He got so gentle. He set the stick down on the shelving like it was a bird with a broken wing, and he took both her hands, and his voice went down into the register he used for her alone.
"Okay," he said. "Okay. How sure— No. Okay. How far— Gigi. Okay."
"Eight weeks," she said. "December. The championship. I did the math with the towels."
Something moved through his face that she declined, for both their sakes, to name. "Are you—" He stopped. Started somewhere safer. "What do you need?"
"That is not the first question, Blake."

"I know." He said it fast, like a man agreeing with a referee. "I know it isn't. I just— Tell me what you need and it's done. Money, a doctor, the good one, not the campus one, whatever it— Gigi, whatever you need."

In her whole life, no one had ever offered Gigi Gavin whatever she needed. Rich people had offered her wages. The academy had offered her a clause-bound scholarship and a cart. Her mother had offered her everything she had, which was love and a phone call. Whatever you need was a sentence from another planet, and it was being said to her by a boy with confetti in his hair while her cart full of his team's towels stood witness, and some traitor part of her — the part that had been invisible since she was six years old — wanted to kneel down in the steam and be grateful for it.
The rest of her stood up straight and watched him go down to the locker room instead.

He came back with the envelope. She knew that envelope. Every athlete at Bridge Water knew that envelope, the way you know things about a kingdom you're paid to launder: Blake Kreave's father made him carry an emergency fund, thick as a paperback, in the back of his locker, because in the Kreave religion money was not wealth, it was preparedness — a sacrament in a bank envelope. Walking-around money, Jack Kreave called it. Five hundred years of money, and it still just meant hush money.
"Take it," Blake said. "For whatever you need. Whatever you decide — I mean that. If you need more, I get more."
"And if I decide—" She let the sentence stand there in the steam, unfinished, where they both could see it.
"Then we figure it out," he said.
"When?"

She watched him understand that she had asked the only question, and she watched the answer assemble itself out of his father's calendar and his mother's seating charts and Layna's smile at the fifty-yard line and four thousand people who had just stood up for him in the dark.
"Not yet," he said. "Gigi. Please. Just — not yet."

It was not cruelty. That was the unbearable part, and she knew it even then: cruelty she could have survived clean. It was arithmetic: she could hear the calendar turning over behind his eyes — the draft talk, the gala, the announcement his mother had been engraving since he was twelve, his father's voice opening a phone call with a score — and she could see him genuinely believe that time was a thing he could hand her, like the envelope, like it would hold still in her pocket and wait politely to become a plan. He believed in not yet the way his family believed in money. It had always worked before. Everything in his life that he had ever pointed not yet at had obligingly stayed unborn.
He did not know it yet, but he was looking at the first thing that wouldn't.

He kissed her forehead, which is a promise and a postponement performed in the same gesture, and then the script called him — there was a party, there was a photograph, there was a girl in a cheer uniform waiting in the light to be his future in public — and he went. He always went. He had never once stayed past the point where the kingdom started asking where he was, and she had built five months of her life inside that fact the way you build a house inside a flood plain, lovingly, and with full knowledge of the river.
The envelope sat on the shelving where he had left it, thick as a paperback, full of his father's preparedness.

Gigi looked at it for a long time. Then she picked it up, and put it in her coat pocket, unopened, and zipped the pocket shut — not because she had decided anything about the money, but because she had decided something about the girl who would one day spend it or hand it back, and that girl was not going to be purchased in an equipment room at midnight, not even by the only hands she had ever wanted on her face.

She locked the laundry. She crossed the empty campus in the cold, past the arena standing dark and enormous over its kingdom, past the gates with the academy's name in iron, and on the other side of the road, right where it always was, the clinic's door burned its one light into the night — judgment-free, patient, open. She had been walking toward it for three hours without admitting it. Her feet knew before she did. They had carried her the long way around her whole life: toward the exit, toward the survivable thing, toward the version of events where Gigi Gavin folds herself small enough to disappear and the kingdom never even hears a sound.

She stopped on the sidewalk, in the neon spill of the sign, with her hand in her pocket around his father's envelope, and she understood that she was not afraid of the door. She was afraid of what she would have to become to walk through it — the girl who let the richest machine on earth quietly pay for her own erasure, who kept her one heartbeat-secret and folded it away like a towel.
Her other hand, without asking her, came to rest flat and low against her stomach, over a fact eight weeks old and entirely unimpressed by the Kreave family calendar.
She walked past the door.

Not righteous. Not decided forever. Just past it — one night, one girl, one small refusal in the dark, with the whole academy asleep behind her and every light in it belonging to somebody else. Everybody at Bridge Water had a price for their silence, and hers had just been delivered in an envelope she couldn't open. Five months she had been his secret, kept in the dark like all the other true things. Now she was carrying a second one — smaller, and louder, and already keeping time like a heart.
How long can you carry a whole person in secret — before the secret starts carrying you?

episodes.title: The Envelope
paras: The envelope lived in her locker, behind the spare uniform, inside the zip pouch where she kept her tips.

Gigi had moved it the morning after — out of the coat pocket it had spent the night zipped into, through the laundry at dawn like contraband, which, she supposed, was exactly what it was: preparedness, smuggled into the one place in the building that was hers by right of nobody else wanting it. Her locker door had a dent in it shaped like somebody's old frustration. The lock worked. That was the entire security apparatus of Gigi Gavin's life, and it had never once failed her, which put it ahead of every person she knew.

She opened the locker four times a shift. She opened the envelope zero times. This was not indecision. Indecision was a rich girl's sport, played with other people's money. This was a policy, arrived at the way all her policies were arrived at: at night, alone, with the arithmetic open on the bed.

His envelope: thick as a paperback, sealed, his father's preparedness, enough money to erase a problem in the Kreave religion's favorite sacrament. Her count of it — because of course she had estimated, the way you estimate a weight you're carrying — said it could buy the good clinic across town, the labs, the vitamins, the bus fare, and a silence so complete it would have its own paperwork. It could buy everything except the one thing it was actually for, which was her disappearance, and that was not a product she was selling at retail.

So on the third morning she bought a second envelope, a plain one, out of the laundry office's supply drawer — "borrowed," the way staff borrowed everything, permanently and without paperwork — and she started her own.

Into hers went the café tips, folded flat, smoothed like they were being tucked in. Five dollars. Nine. A twenty from the booster who tipped like he was apologizing for the century. Her laundry pay went mostly to the bursar's office, which ate on schedule, but the tips were hers in the way almost nothing else was hers: unrecorded, unclaused, earned in smiles she did not mean. By the end of the first week her envelope held forty-one dollars and a decision she hadn't said out loud to anyone, including herself, in a complete sentence.

She did not write anything on his envelope. She did not write anything on hers either. Girls who kept evidence labeled it; girls who survived didn't. She just knew the counts the way she knew everything she owned: exactly, and by heart.
The cart route passed the founders' wall twice a day.

It stood in the arena's main concourse, floor to ceiling, the university's memory in cut stone: the founders, the presidents, the donors with buildings for surnames, and among the civic names — because the arena had been built with the city's money too, and the city always signed its work — MAYOR KLEIN CALHOUN, letters an inch deep, the kind of carving that expected to be read by centuries.

Twice a day, every day, for two years, Gigi Gavin had pushed a laundry cart past her father's name at cart speed, and twice a day her hand had slowed on the handle by exactly the width of one finger. Not a stop. Stops got noticed, and she had been trained out of being noticed by professionals. Just the pause — the cart rolling on, the girl rolling on, the name going past in the stone at the speed of somebody else's importance.

Her mother had taught her that name before she could read the others. That was the whole curriculum, really: one name to know by heart and never say, delivered in a kitchen four hundred miles away by a woman who taught the way weather teaches — constantly, and without caring what it did to the house. Gigi had been reading the wall since she was six years old in every way that mattered. She could have recited the founders in order. She only ever read the one.

Week nine, and the pause cost more than it used to. That was the only difference. The cart rolled on. It always rolled on. She had a job, and the job was the towels, and the towels did not care what was carved in the wall or folded in the locker or growing, at the speed of somebody else's importance, exactly nowhere anyone could see it.
The café shift was where the pregnancy stopped being arithmetic and started being weather.

It was the grill. It had always been the grill — grease, onions, the flat-top's permanent scorched perfume — but week nine had recalibrated her from the inside, and now the smell came off the line like a hand on the back of her neck, patient, pressing down. She worked the register with her jaw set and her breathing rationed through her mouth, and when the rush thinned she traded stations with Misty without a word of explanation, sliding to the cold line where the air came off the refrigerators like mercy.
"Stomach bug's got a season pass, huh?" Misty said, taking the grill tongs like a scepter.
"It's renewing," Gigi said. "Great benefits. Terrible coverage."

Misty, who had been broke in four states and could read a person's whole economy off their shoes, looked at her for exactly one second longer than the joke required, and then — this was why Gigi would have walked into traffic for her, on a schedule and with notice — she turned back to the grill and started performing an elaborate complaint about the dining hall's new oat milk policy, loud enough to cover the sound of Gigi breathing like a woman negotiating with her own body in a walk-in.
Some kindnesses at Bridge Water University were announced at galas. Hers arrived wearing an apron and never once asked to be thanked at a podium.
Pest came in at midnight on Saturday with her shoes in her hand and found Gigi at the desk that was also a table that was also an ironing board, with the envelope open and the tips fanned in rows.
"You're counting money like it's a suspect," Pest said.
"It knows what it did," Gigi said.

Pest set her shoes down with the care of long practice — the scholarship dorm's floors transmitted everything, and the girls on the other side of the wall were studying for futures that had been announced at birth and didn't need the noise. She looked at the rows of small bills for a moment, doing her own arithmetic, which was faster than Gigi's and had no mercy in it at all.
"Tips are up," Pest said. "Kingdom's feeling generous. Must be all that winning."
"Must be."
"You saving for anything, or is this just your personality now?"
Gigi smoothed a five flat with the edge of her hand, the way she smoothed everything, and did not look up. "Rent on a better personality."

"Return policy's terrible," Pest said, and climbed into the top bunk with her textbook, and within four minutes was asleep with it open on her chest like a shield. Pest's gift — the one that made her the most dangerous roommate at Bridge Water University and the only safe one — was that she noticed everything and filed most of it under later. Later had not yet arrived for the envelope. Gigi put the rows away in the dark and did the rest of the count in her head, where she'd always kept the important numbers.
The photograph ran on Sunday, in the paper, above the fold of the sports section like it was news.

The Morris family brunch. A long table at a house with a lawn like a rumor, mimosas at a judicial distance from the underage end, and Blake Kreave seated at the center of it all with Mr. Morris's hand on his shoulder — the hand of a man blessing an investment — and Layna beside him, blond and lit and laughing at something occurring off-camera, in the direction of the rest of her life. The caption, in Priest's most respectful typeface, called them the kingdom's favorite couple and noted the family's generosity to the booster scholarship fund.
Gigi read it in the laundry on her break, standing up, the way staff read everything, with the machines going and somebody else's jersey turning in the steam behind her.

She was in that photograph too. She was just in the part of it that had been taken nine weeks earlier, in December, in the dark, and would develop on a schedule nobody at that table had been consulted about.

She looked at Mr. Morris's hand on his shoulder for a long time. That was the thing about the kingdom's photographs: everything in them was hands. Hands on shoulders, hands on trophies, hands raised in the booster boxes. A whole civilization conducted in the grammar of the approving hand. Somewhere in a stone wall across campus there was a name with no hand attached to it at all, and in a locker behind a spare uniform there was an envelope, and the distance between the photograph and the envelope was the entire length of Bridge Water Ave, and she walked it twice a day at cart speed.
"You look like you're doing math at it," Misty said, from the dryer she wasn't supposed to sit on.
"I am doing math at it," Gigi said. "It adds up. That's the problem."
His text came that night, while she was folding.

The team had gone to some booster thing after the brunch — there was always a booster thing, the kingdom's calendar was an infinite hallway of rooms where he was applauded for existing — and it was late, later than he ever texted her from inside the performance, which told her he'd stepped out of it: a bathroom, a hallway, the two minutes of corridor he'd stolen the way he stole all his real life, in the service spaces between the events of his official one.
did you handle it

No punctuation. He was not a careless texter. The missing question mark was not carelessness; it was a man typing a sentence he could not afford to look at in full sentences, with punctuation, like it was a real question being asked by a real person of the only person alive who knew what it cost.

Gigi stood in the laundry with the phone lit in her hand and a half-folded towel over her arm, and she did the thing she had not known she was going to do until she did it: she answered him three times, in the composition window, with her whole chest.

episodes.title: Thank You
paras: Yes.

One word. A lie so small it could live anywhere. She read it sitting there in its little gray field and understood that it was not small at all — it was a country, and if she sent it she would have to live in it, fold its towels, breathe its air, raise the whole arrangement inside it. She deleted it.
I need more time.

True, and useless, and worse: it was his sentence. It was "not yet" wearing her clothes. The day she started answering him in his own grammar would be the day she became staff in her own life. Deleted.
No.

One word again. The detonating one. No — I didn't handle it. No — there is still a heartbeat in this building that you paid to un-happen and it's keeping time in the laundry. No — come down here and look at the thing you actually did, in the only room where you're a person, and let's both stop performing the version where time is a substance you can hand me. Her thumb hovered over the send arrow for the length of one full machine cycle, and the whole future stood there with her in the steam, patient as water.
Then she deleted that too, and locked the phone, and finished folding the towel.

She told herself it was because a text message was no way to say it. She told herself midnight in a laundry room was no time to say it. She told herself — the telling was elaborate, thorough, extremely well-folded — that she was protecting the telling for the right room, the right hour, the version where she could watch his face do the three things it had done the first time and know which one lasted.

What she did not tell herself was the thing she already knew, standing there with her hands in other people's warm towels: that the silence was already an answer. That it had been traveling ahead of her for ten full seconds, up the service stairwell of his night, and arriving.
His reply came eleven minutes later.
thank you
get some rest. long week.

She read it twice. She could hear the exhale in it — eleven minutes of a boy in a stolen hallway, watching a screen stay empty, building the only possible house out of the emptiness: she handled it. It's over. We survived it. He had read her silence the way everyone read Gigi Gavin: as the absence of a problem. It was the world's oldest misreading of her, performed now by the one person who had ever claimed to see her, and she had handed him the empty page and let him write it.

She could correct it tomorrow. That was the thought she took to bed, up the four flights to the scholarship dorm, past the radiator that clanked all winter, into the room where Pest was asleep with a textbook on her face. Tomorrow. She could walk down to the equipment room tomorrow and say it in the room where he was a person, and it would be a hard hour and a clean one.

She set no alarm for it. She told no one to remind her. She lay in the dark and listened to the building settle, and the hand that was not holding the phone came to rest, on its own initiative, low on her stomach, the way it had started doing in the dark like it had its own opinions now, and she let it stay.
Tomorrow, she thought, and folded the word up small, and put it in the place where she kept everything she intended to survive.
The next afternoon she saw what her silence had bought him.

Practice load-in, the tunnel full of equipment and noise, and Blake Kreave coming through it loose — that was the word her body used before her mind could vote on it — loose, laughing at something Franky was performing at full volume, a ball spinning on his finger, his shoulders down out of his ears for the first time since February. The kingdom's boy, restored to factory settings. He'd slept. You could see the sleep on him like weather that had changed.

He passed within arm's reach of her cart, close enough that the edge of his sleeve brushed the towels, and he did not look at her — of course he did not look at her; looking at her in the tunnel, in daylight, in front of the whole traveling circus was not an item on any menu his life offered — but she heard him say it to Franky, easy, tossing the ball, meaning spring ball and a dozen other things and only one real one:
"Told you. We're fine."

We're fine. She pushed the cart the length of the tunnel with the sentence riding on it like a passenger. He had already moved in. That was the part nobody warned you about in the arithmetic of the unanswered text: the silence hadn't just let him believe it — it had let him furnish the belief, hang pictures in it, sleep a full night inside it with his shoulders down. Every day she waited now was not a day before the telling. It was a day deeper into his relief, and the telling, when it came, would not just be news. It would be an eviction.
She folded that fact and put it where she kept the important numbers, and went to her shift.
In the morning she did the math on the back of a café receipt, standing at the bus stop on Bridge Water Ave with her shift in one hour and the whole bright kingdom waking up across the street.

The good clinic — the one across town, the one Blake had offered with such desperate fluency, the good one, not the campus one — charged by the visit and charged for the labs, and the numbers she assembled out of the clinic's own cheerful website, read on a cracked screen at 6 a.m., came to a figure that her envelope could not yet say out loud. Her envelope, after the weekend's tips were folded in and smoothed flat and tucked in like they were being put to bed by somebody who loved them, held sixty-three dollars.
The clinic wanted a hundred and forty before it would so much as confirm what she already knew in her own body, on her own schedule, for free.

She stood there doing the rich arithmetic of the poor, which is the same arithmetic with the answers in a different order, and she made the decision that poor girls made every day in every town with a name: she triaged. Not the visit. Not yet — that word again, hers this time, and she heard it in her own voice and didn't flinch from the family resemblance. The vitamins first. The vitamins were fourteen dollars and they were a decision in a direction, and direction, unlike confirmation, was something her envelope could afford.

The pharmacy sat on Bridge Water Ave, on her side of the street, where the awnings were older and the signs didn't match. To reach it from the gates she had to walk past the clinic — the near one, the all-night one, the one with the door that burned its single light into the dark like an eye that never judged anybody. She had walked past it once before, in the cold, with an arrangement breaking in her ears. This time she walked past it in daylight, at errand speed, with a list.

It cost less than she expected, being a girl with a list. The pharmacist didn't look up twice. On the counter by the register, in a wire rack of free information, sat a leaflet from the good clinic across town — services, fees, a photograph of a door with light coming through it, and the words confidential appointments in a typeface designed to lower blood pressure. She took one. Information was the one currency she had never once run out of, and a leaflet was not an appointment; it committed her to nothing; it was only paper, and paper was her native element. She folded it into her coat, small, the way she folded everything that mattered.

The bottle rode home in her coat pocket, in the exact pocket where his father's envelope had spent its one night, and if the symmetry was a joke, it was the kind her life specialized in: dry, and on her.

That night, in the laundry, with the machines going and the kingdom asleep above her, she put fourteen dollars' worth of vitamins in her locker next to an envelope of uncounted thousands she would not open, and she folded the pharmacy receipt small and put it in her own envelope with the money, because receipts were what you kept when you intended to prove, someday, to somebody, that you had been careful with what was yours.

Sixty-three dollars. A bottle of vitamins. A name in a wall she passed twice a day. A silence standing where an answer should be, growing, like everything else in her keeping, on a schedule nobody had consulted her about.
If a lie is only a silence you let stand, who does it belong to — the one who needed it, or the one who kept it?

episodes.title: Blind Item
paras: The night laundry shift was the best shift at Bridge Water University, and Gigi had not started trading for it until February, which told you everything about what February had done to her scheduling.

The machines were free at night. The steam had the room to itself. Nobody's mother called the laundry at 2 a.m. to discuss a son's minutes, nobody's booster wandered down looking for the facilities manager, and the whole bright civilization of the arena went dark above her like a theater after the audience remembers it has somewhere better to be. She could fold in peace. She could be sick in peace, too, which — at week ten — had become a scheduling consideration with its own seniority. Her body had started keeping hours no roster recognized: it woke her at two with the nausea already standing in the room like a bailiff, and it did not negotiate, and it did not care that she had a mid-term. So she had stopped fighting it and staffed it. If she was going to be awake in the dark with her stomach keeping count, she might as well be paid in clean machines and empty corridors.
She told herself it was strategy. Some of it even was.

That night the building was doing its off-hours sounds — pipes, ice machine, the far-off tick of cooling concrete — and she was halfway through the basketball whites when the arena door sighed, one floor up and half a building away, in the particular way that meant a person and not the wind.

She should have stayed in the laundry. She knew the roster of sounds the way she knew the counts in her envelope, and a person in the arena at 2 a.m. was not her business, not her department, not her problem. She went anyway, up the service stairs with a stack of towels over her arm as an alibi, because alibis were a reflex by now, and because some animal part of her that had never once consulted her policy manual already knew whose insomnia walked this building at night.

He was in the seats. Mid-arena, halfway up the empty bowl, in sweats and a hoodie with the hood down, a ball resting in his lap like something he'd been given to hold and forgotten to use. Not shooting. Not training. Just sitting in the exact center of the kingdom, in the dark, in the one hour when it didn't perform, looking at the court where the lights were off and the banners hung like sleeping animals.
Blake Kreave, alone in it. All of it. His.

Gigi stood in the service vomitory with the towels against her chest and watched the most announced boy in the state be nobody, at length, in the dark, and she understood that she was looking at the only other person at Bridge Water University whose real life was scheduled around the performance the way hers was — except the whole building was built for his performance, and her job was to launder its costumes, and he was sitting in the middle of the difference looking like it weighed exactly as much as her side of it did.

She took the photograph before she had decided to. That was the truth of it, and she kept it in the honest ledger she kept for herself: the phone was up, the screen's small light bloomed in the dark, the shutter made its lying little sound — off, she'd set it off months ago, the way you set everything off when your life is a service corridor — and the picture was taken. Him, small and lit by the exit signs' green spill, the ball in his lap, the bowl of empty seats around him like a tide gone out.
She looked at it a long time. It was the saddest true thing she owned.

She did not send it anywhere. She put the phone away and took the towels back down to the steam, and she folded the basketball whites with the photograph in her pocket, and for two days it stayed there doing what true things do in pockets: getting heavier.

The next night he came down at 2 a.m. the way he always came down — out of the dark building, two coffees, the real laugh saved up all day like money — and for one whole hour the arrangement held the way it had held since September. He sat on the equipment cage he wasn't supposed to sit on and told her about the film session, about Castro's face, about the scout from State who'd asked his father — not him, his father — whether the Kreave boy slept well, like he was livestock being vetted for temperament. "I said I sleep like a baby," he told her. "Dad handled it. 'The boy sleeps like a rock.' It's in the file now. Official. I sleep like a rock."
"Do you?" Gigi said.
"You've seen the rock," he said, and tipped his head at the ceiling, at the dark arena above them both, and grinned the grin that was only ever hers.

Her phone was in her apron pocket, against her hip, with the photograph in it — him, twelve hours earlier, not sleeping, not a rock, a boy in an empty bowl of seats with a ball in his lap like an apology. All night it sat there between them like a third person in the room, and she understood, with the particular clarity that only ever visited her in steam, that she had crossed a line so fine she couldn't see it in the dark: for five months she had kept Blake Kreave's secrets from the world. Now she was keeping one from him.

It felt different. That was the whole report she could have filed: it felt different in the hand, like a towel folded wrong. She kept secrets the way other people kept house — it was her function, her trade, her religion — and she had never once felt the weight of one go uneven before. She sat in the bleach-smell with the boy she loved telling her the truth about a lie his father had told a scout, and she smiled in the right places, and she said nothing about the photograph, and the nothing had a texture she could feel with her whole body.
She told herself she would delete it. She told herself twice, to make it a policy.
What spent it was a Tuesday, at the café, at the kingdom's lunch hour.

Steff was holding court at the corner table — the squad's table, the one with the light — performing the squad's new concern, which was Blake's focus. It was done in the kingdom's kindest register, the one that cut deepest: the worried voices, the tilted heads, the isn't-he-different-lately, the someone-should-talk-to-him, the whole machine of concern that existed, Gigi had come to understand, so that a boy could be dismantled in public and everyone involved could call it care. Layna sat in the middle of it saying almost nothing, which was its own kind of information, and Steff — reaching, the way she reached — said, "I mean, where does he even go? At night? He's never anywhere anymore. It's like he's got a whole other—" and laughed, and the table laughed, and the sentence finished itself in four different imaginations.
Gigi, refilling the water glasses at the kingdom's elbow, heard her own knowledge get spent by people who knew nothing, at the price of nothing, for sport.

She thought about the photograph. She thought about what it actually showed: not a boy with a secret girl. A boy alone in the dark in the place that owned him, unable to sleep in the palace. True. Harmless — she audited it twice for harm, the way she audited everything, and it passed: it proved an ache, not an affair. It indicted the crown, not the king's whereabouts. It was, by the standards of the economy she lived in, almost a kindness: it would tell the kingdom its golden boy was human, at 2 a.m., in a language the kingdom charged admission to read.
That night, in the laundry, with the machines going, she audited the photograph the way she audited everything she was about to spend.

What it showed: a boy, alone, in the arena he owned, at an hour when owning it was worthless. What it did not show: the equipment room. The corridor. Her. There was no door in it, no threshold, no evidence that anyone had ever been down those stairs with him — the affair was not in the frame, and she checked the frame three times, corner to corner, the way she checked a med cabinet or a brake line in the stories she told herself about other people's carelessness. The angle was the only flaw. The photograph had been taken from the service vomitory, at staff height, from the one mouth of the arena that only staff used at night. If it ever printed, anyone who knew the building — and one boy knew the building the way she did — could pace off exactly where the photographer had been standing.

She stood in the steam and priced that, honestly, the whole price: if he ever saw it in print, he would know the height it was taken from. He would know a staff ghost had been in the dark with him. He might even, eventually, count the ghosts.

She sent it anyway. That was the part she wrote down in the honest ledger: not that she hadn't seen the risk. That she'd seen it, entire, and decided the kingdom hearing its king was human was worth being countable.

The account she made had never had her name on it anywhere — a throwaway address, a password she'd forget on purpose. The caption she wrote three times. The first said too much about the sender: deleted. The second said too much about the boy: deleted. The third she kept, because it said only what the photograph said, and nothing she felt:
2 a.m. He sits alone in it.
She did not sign it. She did not have to. Unsigned was her native language.
The paper came out on Thursday, and Priest did not print the photograph.

Gigi understood what that meant before she finished the item, standing in the laundry with the paper in her hands and somebody's practice gear steaming itself dry behind her. He could have printed it. A photograph of the king alone in his empty arena at 2 a.m. would have sold the issue out by lunch — the whole kingdom fighting to look at its own sadness in print. He'd held it instead. He'd printed only the words.
WHICH golden boy was photographed alone at 2 a.m. in his empty arena — and what is the crown too heavy to say out loud?

Eleven words of question, no name, no picture, and at the bottom of the column, in the paper's smallest type, a note that this was the first installment of a series the paper was calling KINGDOM CRACKING. Which meant Priest wasn't spending what she'd sent him. He was investing it. He was building a file the way you build a fire — slowly, with the good wood saved for when the room was full.

episodes.title: Kingdom Cracking
paras: She had fed the machine exactly one true thing, and the machine, being a machine, had not done the simple thing with it. It had opened an account.
By Friday she could read the item's blast radius off the building like scorch marks, because reading buildings was her whole education and the staff saw everything first.

Blake came down the tunnel an hour before practice instead of twenty minutes — early enough that the corridor was still hers — and stood at the equipment-room door for a count of four with his hand not quite raised, like a man checking whether a house he used to live in still had his key in the lock. The door was shut. The light was off. Whatever he was looking for — the ghost of a witness, the geography of who could have been where — he didn't find it, and Franky arrived at a shout, and the moment closed over him like water. But Gigi, watching from the laundry doorway with a basket against her hip and her face set to furniture, had seen the thing she'd actually bought with her photograph: the king, in daylight, counting exits.

Layna read it at the squad's table and went quiet in a way that rearranged the air around her. Steff, mid-performance, watched her friend's smile arrive half a second after the joke did — installed, not felt — and even Steff, who had never filed an unspoken thing in her life, looked down at her food and let the moment pass unmonetized. Whatever Layna Morris was thinking about a photograph of her boyfriend awake and alone at 2 a.m., in a building full of rooms he wasn't in with her, she was thinking it at full price, in silence, like a professional. And when the squad stood up to go, Gigi watched her fold the paper — not crumple it, not leave it for the staff to clear, fold it, twice, precisely, and put it in her own bag. Layna Morris kept things. It was the first item Gigi ever filed on her, and she filed it carefully, the way you file weather you intend to dress for later.

Manny read it in the locker room and laughed too loud at it, the way men laugh at weather reports in the path of the storm, and then — Gigi heard this one third-hand, through the equipment manager, who heard everything and repeated it as inventory — he spent lunch on the phone in the stairwell with his voice at the pitch of a man discussing money he did not have with people who did not offer extensions. The blind item had asked what the crown was too heavy to say out loud, and Manny, who owed money in three directions, had apparently heard the question as addressed to him personally.

And Steff — Steff performed the most total disinterest Gigi had ever seen outside a deposition, while being able, by dinner, to recite the item word for word, including the punctuation. Whatever 2 a.m. of Steff's own the item had stepped on, she had buried it under eleven exact words and a smile, and only the recitation gave her away.
Four people. Four secrets. One true photograph, of none of them — of a boy sitting alone in the dark, which was the whole story and also, somehow, about everybody.

Misty read it in the laundry on her break, holding the paper at arm's length like it might be contagious, and delivered her review to the steam. "Kingdom Cracking," she read. "Installment one. He's going to need a bigger file." She turned the paper sideways. "Photographed alone at 2 a.m. In his own arena. The tragedy. Somebody should check on the staff — we could've told him the king doesn't sleep, we have the towels to prove it, there's a whole load comes down at midnight smelling like regret and energy drinks." She set the paper down. "Whoever sent that in knew where he'd be."
"Everybody knows where he'd be," Gigi said. "He's the king. He's always here."
"Uh-huh," said Misty, in the tone of a woman placing a disbelief in a labeled envelope for later, and went back to her fries.

That night Gigi did the week's bookkeeping in the dorm with Pest asleep above her and the radiator clanking its one note. The envelope: forty-nine dollars, after the vitamins. The notebook: a small clean 10 written in the margin of her biology notes, where the week's number went now, one digit a week, the only honest calendar she kept. On her phone, with the brightness down, the good clinic's booking page — the one across town, the one with the cheerful website — asked her to choose a date and a time and a reason for the visit, and showed her the fee for the first appointment like it was nothing, like a hundred and forty dollars was a number that happened to other people accidentally.

The Kingdom Cracking file had opened on a Thursday. Her first clinic visit had come due the same week, and gone by unbooked, and the two facts sat on the desk in front of her in the dark — the file she had started on purpose, growing on schedule, and the appointment she hadn't started at all — and she closed the booking page and wrote nothing in the margin about either of them.

Gigi folded towels and did the arithmetic she was best at. She had aimed at one thing: the kingdom would know its king was human. She had hit four other things and the one thing besides, and the one thing was the one that cost her. Because Blake Kreave — frightened now, counting the tunnel's exits, arriving early to stand at a shut door — did not come down at 2 a.m. anymore.

The corridor hour ended without an announcement. The equipment room went back to being a room. The next night, and the next, the arena stayed dark and empty at the hour when it used to hold the only honest version of him she had, and Gigi folded the basketball whites in the steam and understood that she had done a new thing, a thing she hadn't done in all the months of holding his secrets and her own: she had spent one. And the machine had taken her one true thing and opened a file with it, and files, unlike boys, do not get frightened and stop coming downstairs. Files just grow.

She passed the press table on Friday's last run, when the arena was emptying its light into the parking lots, and Priest was still there, typing with the calm of a man taking dictation at an execution, filing installment two of the kingdom's memory while it was still warm.
"Busy week," Gigi said, because staff say things to furniture and Priest was, by common agreement, furniture with a byline.

"Submissions are up," Priest said, without looking up. "Anonymous ones especially. Very healthy for a paper. People trust us with the truth when they don't have to sign it." The typing didn't pause. "You hear confession long enough, Gavin, you stop needing names. The sins have handwriting."
She pushed her cart into the dark with her heart going like a snare drum and her face set to furniture, and she did not hurry, because hurrying was a signature too.
His text came at eleven, while the last loads were turning: paper's bored. slow news week. Then, a moment later: you'd tell me if i should care about that, right?

She stood in the steam and read it for what it was — a boy performing unbothered at a girl whose whole job was knowing what he looked like bothered — and she typed back the truth, the whole of it that could survive a screen: It's a slow news week, Blake. Get some sleep. She watched him receive the comfort of a person who had personally arranged his fright, and she felt the new texture again, the towel folded wrong, the weight gone uneven: she was managing him now. Gently, kindly, expertly, the way the kingdom managed everybody — and she had learned it at home, and it fit her hand like it had been made there.

She looked at the photograph on her phone that night — his small lit figure in the empty bowl, the tide gone out around him — and she did not delete it. Deleting was a kind of evidence too, and besides: it was still the saddest true thing she owned, and now it was also the most expensive.
When you've fed a machine exactly one true thing, how do you keep it from asking for the next?

episodes.title: Receipts
paras: She walked to work down Bridge Water Ave at the hour when the street belonged to nobody.

The scholarship dorm stood on her side of it, four floors of radiator clank and other people's announced futures, and the university stood on the other — gates, lawns, the arena's dark glass roof catching nothing yet. Between the two, the avenue ran its one honest shift: the diner's neon buzzing awake, the early bus sighing at the stop, a man hosing the sidewalk in front of a shuttered bar, the pharmacy's grate still down. Her side of Bridge Water woke up working. The other side woke up announced. She crossed at the corner by the clinic — the near clinic, the all-night one, whose famous door in daylight was only a door, painted institutional green, with a taped schedule curling in the window and a woman with a stroller going in ordinary as groceries — and the ordinariness of it at 5 a.m. did something to her chest that the neon at midnight never had. In the dark the door had been a verdict. In the morning it was an errand other women ran. She put it in the ledger under things she was not ready to know yet, and she went to work.

The laundry at 6 a.m. was all steam and first light, and Gigi had been in it since five, because the basketball whites from the weekend tournament had come down in a state that suggested the team had celebrated directly into them.

She was pulling the last load out of the big washer — warm, heavy, smelling of bleach and other people's effort — when the room tilted. Not spun. Tilted, gently, with the same boat-deciding courtesy her body had used on her beside Misty's dryer a month ago, except this time it kept going, past the point where courtesy ended, and the floor started being a place she needed to negotiate with. She got one hand on the cart. She got the other on the washer's warm flank. The towels slid. She sat down — not fell, sat, with whatever dignity a controlled descent could claim — on the laundry floor, in the steam, among the fallen whites, and waited for the room to remember it was a room.
"You sat down," Misty said from the door, with her bag over her shoulder and her voice very level. "You never sit down. I've known you two years. Sitting down is not in your product line."
"Gravity's doing inspections," Gigi said. "Union rules. Everybody down."

Misty crossed the room without hurrying, which was how you knew she was frightened, and crouched, and put the back of her hand against Gigi's forehead with the proprietary air of a woman who had raised siblings on two continents' worth of no money. "You're not hot. You're gray. Gray is worse. Gray is a color they don't even sell here, everybody's golden." She produced, from the depths of her bag, a granola bar of true geological age. "Eat. And before you say the bug — the bug has been renewing since February, Gavin. Bugs don't renew. Subscriptions renew. Whatever this is, it has your name on the account."

Gigi ate the granola bar sitting on the floor of the laundry, in the steam, in her uniform, and it was — she would think about this later, at length, in the dark — the most cared-for she had felt in many weeks, and it had cost a granola bar and a crouch and absolutely no questions that required lying. Misty asked nothing. Misty just sat down on the floor too, in her own uniform, with her back against the other washer, and ate the second ancient granola bar herself, in solidarity, like a woman at a picnic in a war zone.
"Floor's warm," Misty said.
"Best seat in the building," Gigi said. "Don't tell the boosters. They'll put a plaque on it."

Misty ran her loads for twenty minutes while Gigi lay on the staff-room cot with one arm over her eyes, officially inventorying the annex, which was a lie Misty had constructed out of whole cloth in under four seconds and defended, when the weekend supervisor drifted through, with the serene authority of a woman reading scripture: "Inventory. Annex. She's counting the annex." The supervisor, who did not know where the annex was and suspected there wasn't one, drifted out again. Gigi lay in the dark of her own arm and listened to somebody else fold her towels, badly, out of love, and understood that she would have to find a way to survive being cared for in installments, because the alternative — the whole truth, all at once, in any room — was a door she had already walked past twice.

Week eleven had redrawn the map of the building by smell. Gigi navigated it the way sailors navigated by stars: the café grill was a storm to be skirted; the equipment room's bleach had gone from perfume to weather warning; the laundry's steam, which had been her element for two years, had started closing over her head like water. Her body was revising her relationship with every room she worked in, on its own schedule, without consulting the roster, and it was doing it in front of people whose whole job was not noticing her — a mercy, she kept telling herself. The help could turn gray in a steam cloud and the kingdom would chalk it up to atmosphere.

What she could no longer do was the arithmetic out loud. The clinic had stopped being a number she rehearsed and become a door she walked around, and she had started furnishing the walk-around with reasons that had edges: a visit was a record. A record had her name in a system, and a date, and a reason coded in a cheerful drop-down menu, and systems at Bridge Water University were read by people — by Finch, if you asked him nicely; by the university, if it ever asked itself. She believed this reason. She also heard it, the way you hear a floorboard in a house you know: it held weight, but it wasn't the joist. The joist was simpler and uglier and she kept it in the honest ledger where she kept everything true: the good clinic across town was where a girl went to be told, in a room with a door that closed, exactly what she was doing. And she was not ready to hear it in a voice that wasn't her own.

So the envelope grew. Sixty-eight dollars. Seventy-one. The vitamins rode in her locker like a tiny standing army. And the body, which had not agreed to any of this scheduling, kept its own calendar in its own ink, and had begun, at week eleven, to present its accounts in public.
Professor Torres's biology class met at ten in a room with real windows, which was why Gigi had always liked it: it was the one room in the kingdom where the light wasn't performing.

Torres lectured the way she did everything — like a woman reading a map she respected. The reproduction unit had been announced the week before with a straight face and a syllabus, and the class had received it with the full spectrum of university maturity, from the boy who asked if it would be on the exam to the girl who live-texted it. Gigi sat in the third row with her notebook open and her week-count ledger in its margin, and on Tuesday Torres put the development chart on the screen, week by week, in drawings the color of soft fruit.

Week eleven, the drawing said. The size of a fig. A heart that had divided into chambers and was beating at twice the mother's rate, a spine like a string of pearls, the beginnings — the drawing's word was buds — of everything.

Gigi looked at the fig on the screen and did the conversion the way she did every conversion now, instantly and without permission: a fig, somewhere under her ribs, beating at twice her rate. She had not known the rate fact. Her own heart, being informed of it, immediately attempted a demonstration.

"Imagine being pregnant at Bridge Water," said the boy two seats down, at the volume young men use when they are certain the room agrees with them. "You'd have to, like, transfer. To State." The laugh came up around him on schedule, warm and unexamined, and somebody said State like it was a country you got deported to, and the laugh went around again, better fed.

"Half the people who have ever sat in that chair," Torres said, not loudly, from the front of the room, where she had not looked up from the chart, "were somebody's surprise. Sit up, please. All of you. It improves the circulation you are currently failing to learn about."

The laugh died the way laughs die when a teacher doesn't raise her voice. The boy sat up. The chart advanced. Gigi kept her seat and her face arranged in the expression she had been issued at birth — pleasant, unbothered, furniture — and did not hate him, particularly. That was the part she would remember: the joke was weather. She had grown up in a climate where her existence was the punchline of exactly this joke, told in kitchens and at bus stops by men who never once checked who was in earshot of it — men appraising the world in the hearing of the girls it was about, her whole childhood's background music — and the weather at Bridge Water University was better funded, that was all. Better funded, and it charged tuition.

At the break she went down the service stairwell, the one the students didn't use, and was sick in a mop sink with the door shut, quietly and professionally, the way she had been sick for six weeks: no audience, no event, nothing to file. She rinsed the sink. She washed her face with cold water at the tap and dried it on a paper towel and checked the mirror, which was staff-grade and honest: a girl looking back at her, gray at the edges, holding.

She thought about the fig. Twice her rate. It was the first fact about the baby that had arrived with no price attached, and she stood in a service stairwell with wet hands and held it like money she hadn't earned.
"Okay," she said to the stairwell, to the fig, to nobody. "Okay. Heard."

Then she went back up and took the rest of the lecture sitting very straight, sit up, please, all of you, and her notes were immaculate, and if her hand shook once on the word chambers she covered it by underlining it twice, like emphasis, like a girl who just really cared about biology.
"Gigi. Stay a moment."

episodes.title: Office Hours
paras: The room emptied around her in the usual river — bags, laughter, the boy who sat up straighter now on principle — and Gigi stayed, because there was no version of leaving that wasn't a signature.

Torres's office was small and aggressively unrenovated, down the hall from the lab, with a plant on the sill that had clearly been told it would not be watered on a schedule and had decided to live anyway. There was a clipboard on the desk. There is always a clipboard; Torres had care with a clipboard, it was her instrument, and Gigi's eyes went to it the way they went to all instruments in rooms where she was about to be measured.

"Sit," Torres said. "You missed the lab write-up on Thursday. You do not miss lab write-ups. I have two years of evidence." She set the clipboard down — face down, which Gigi registered the way you register a door being deliberately unlatched — and poured water from her own bottle into a paper cup and put it in front of her, the way you put water in front of anyone whose body you'd been watching change its testimony for a month. "Drink. Slowly. It's a biology requirement."
Gigi drank. The office was quiet in the way of rooms with no performance scheduled in them. Outside the window, the quad was doing its noon impression of a brochure.

"You stand like furniture now," Torres said. "You always stood a little like furniture — it's the job, I know the job, don't perform surprise — but lately you stand like furniture that's holding something up. And you sit down in my lectures like a person defusing herself. And the write-up." She folded her hands. She did not ask a question. That was the thing Gigi would turn over later, in the dark, like a coin she couldn't spend: Torres, who asked questions for a living, who could have asked the one question in the building with the training behind it, arranged the entire conversation so that no question in it required Gigi to lie.

"Whatever it is, it's yours," Torres said. "To tell or not tell. I want that understood as coming first, because everything else I say is worthless if that isn't first." She nodded at the cup. "Second is fluids. Third is that my door has hours posted on it and hours that aren't, and you are a member of the scholarship cohort, which means this office is, among other things, contractually yours." She said it dryly, like reading off the chart. "And fourth — " She looked at her then, not at the clipboard, not at the plant, at her, with the whole of her attention, which was a rarer instrument than any in the lab. "The body keeps the receipts, Gigi. Whatever you've been telling it to wait — it isn't waiting. It's keeping count where anyone trained can see it. I can see it. So drink the water, and don't insult either of us by telling me it's a stomach bug with a season pass."
The room went very quiet. Somewhere in Gigi's chest a door she kept triple-locked did the thing it did at 2 a.m. in equipment rooms: it recognized a person.
She opened her mouth.

She could feel the sentence arrive — whole, grammatical, in her own voice, the first true one she would have said above stairs in her entire enrollment: Professor Torres, I'm — and she watched it approach the air the way she'd watched Blake's face do three things in a tunnel, and what came out of her, in the end, with the water cup in her hand and the kindest woman in the building waiting without one single lever in her hand, was:
"Can I make up the write-up Friday? I have the data. I just didn't — I ran out of week."

"Friday," Torres said, after a moment in which she accepted the answer the way you accept weather you can't grade. "Bring the data. Bring the receipts." She said it lightly, like a joke about homework, and let it be one, and Gigi understood that she had just been given the rarest thing the kingdom had ever issued her: a door she was allowed not to walk through, held open by somebody who would not count the not-walking against her.

She walked out with the office-hours card in her pocket. It was printed on stock the color of pale money. Office hours, and the unposted hours, in Torres's small exact handwriting, added underneath in pen: or the lab, most afternoons.
She thought about it all evening, in the laundry, in the café line, in the dorm with Pest asleep and the radiator making its one argument.

Not telling wasn't fear. She had audited that on the walk down from the office, and the audit came back clean in a way that frightened her more than fear would have: she hadn't stayed silent because Torres might report her, or price her, or join the long line of adults who had appraised Gigi Gavin and found her manageable. She'd stayed silent because the secret was the only property she owned outright. Everything else — the scholarship, the dorm room, the uniform, the boy — came with a clause, a calendar, a seating chart, somebody else's name in cut stone on the wall of it. The baby was hers the way nothing in her life had ever been hers, unshared and unannounced and unpriced by any office, and to tell it above stairs — even to a kind woman, even into a kindness with no levers — would be to give it an address in the kingdom. Things with addresses in the kingdom got managed. She had watched it happen to weather systems smaller than this.

That was the clean audit. The honest ledger, underneath it, kept a second entry, in smaller writing: she hadn't told because telling would have made it real in a room with windows, and real things in rooms with windows could be grieved, and planned for, and helped — and she did not know how to be helped by anyone who wasn't holding two coffees in the dark. Cruelty she had forms for. Kindness arrived with no paperwork at all, and she stood in front of it the way she stood in front of every unpriced thing: empty-handed, counting exits.

Pest was awake when she came in, which was irregular enough to be its own announcement — sitting up in the top bunk with her textbook closed, watching Gigi empty her pockets onto the desk the way she did every night: keys, phone, the envelope, and now a pale printed card that hadn't been in the rotation before.
"Torres card," Pest said. "Office hours. Fancy. She hand those to all her students or just the ones who sit down on her floor?"
"I didn't sit on her floor. I sat on the laundry floor. Different department."

"Multi-department sitting. Very scholarship cohort." Pest swung her legs over the bunk's edge and regarded her with the unhurried attention of a girl reading a document she intended to remember verbatim. "You seeing a lot of Professor Torres these days, Gavin."
"She's my professor, Pest. It's a whole system. There's a schedule and everything."

"Uh-huh." Pest lay back and reopened her textbook, and the subject was closed the way roadwork is closed — cones up, traffic rerouted, men with equipment clearly scheduled to return. Gigi knew that tone. She had been deploying that tone since September. It was the sound of a file being opened by somebody who loved you and intended, eventually, to know what was in it.

That night she opened the notebook to the margin where the weeks lived and wrote 11 in her small clean hand, and underneath it — for the first time, because Torres had given her the grammar for it whether she wanted it or not — she started the second column. The body's own ledger, in the body's own categories.
Sick: the nights. All of them, now. Ate: a granola bar, on a floor. Stood: mostly. Sat: once, involuntarily. Heart: twice hers, apparently, and keeping up.

Receipts, in other words. She was keeping them the way she'd been taught everything was kept: quietly, exactly, and in a book nobody else would ever be allowed to audit. The baby had exactly one bookkeeper on earth, and she wrote the numbers in a margin, and she closed the notebook, and she put Torres's card in her envelope with the money — sixty-eight dollars, seventy-one, and one pale printed rectangle that was the strangest currency she'd ever held: an offer, from a woman with a clipboard, that didn't have to be spent to be worth something.
She didn't know what it was worth. She only knew it was the first thing in the envelope that wasn't for the baby or against the kingdom, and that she had carried it home like money anyway.
When the only safe person is the one you can never tell, what exactly is the kindness for?

episodes.title: Extra Reps
paras: The med room was the only room at Bridge Water University that Gigi was ever invited to be careful in.

It sat off the training room with a door that locked from the inside and a cabinet that locked from everywhere, and twice a week, on the rotation she had requested in February and never explained, the cabinet was hers to count. Bandages by the box. Tape by the roll. The cold packs, the braces, the wraps that smelled of every ankle they had ever held. And in the locked section, behind the second key, the labeled bottles: the kingdom's chemistry, each one with a player's name typed on pharmacy paper, each one prescribed by a doctor whose name the players pronounced like a password.

She had asked for the rotation the way she asked for everything — sideways, with a trade instead of a reason. The equipment manager got two of her Saturday mornings; she got Tuesday and Friday counts and a clipboard with her initials in the log, twice a week, in ink. What she had wanted, in February, was information, which was the only currency she had never run out of: what the room held, what it cost, what a person did in this building when a body went wrong at 2 a.m. and the campus clinic was a dark office and the good clinic across town wanted a hundred and forty dollars to open its mouth. A girl in her position — though the position had no name yet, not even in her own ledger — did her reconnaissance the way staff did everything. Quietly. With a clipboard. As a favor to the roster.

What the room held, she now knew by count and by heart. It held the means of her own emergencies, most of them priced beyond her envelope, and it held something she had not gone looking for: Jacob's season, in a bottle with his name typed on it, waiting for somebody's hand to decide what it meant.

Jacob was the kingdom's other story that spring — the comeback, the feel-good column Priest kept warming up in his notebook. A starting spot on the spring depth chart, an ankle sprain in the last week of winter workouts, two weeks of the pool and the table and the trainers' hands, and now the long public march back: Jacob, taping his own ankle at the same bench every morning with the concentration of a man defusing himself; Jacob, running his first cuts at three-quarter speed while the coaches pretended not to watch and watched; Jacob, whose mother drove in from two counties away to stand at the fence for practices she was not supposed to attend, because some families announced their love and some just drove it in and parked it at the fence.

He was not unkind to the staff. That was the worst of it, later — the part her bookkeeping kept itemizing. He held doors with his crutch in the bad weeks. He said thank you to the room in general, which in the kingdom counted as a form of address. When the hot water in the training room ran brown for a day, he was the one who told the freshmen not to drink it, loudly, like a public service. He was, in the taxonomy Gigi kept for the kingdom's men, one of the decent ones — which only meant his file was thinner, not that he was safe from the arithmetic she was about to do on him.

That Monday he was at his bench at seven with the tape already out, rebuilding the ankle the way he rebuilt it every morning, wrap over wrap, with the patience of a man who intended to be believed. The head trainer stood over him with the spring showcase sheet in his hand — the Saturday the scouts' stand-ins came, the Saturday the chart got inked — and read the week's plan aloud like a sentence being handed down: walk-throughs Tuesday, three-quarter speed Thursday, full session when the ankle said so.
"Ankle says so when I say so," Jacob said, without looking up from the tape.
"Ankle's not the one with the clipboard, son."
"No," Jacob said, and grinned up at him with the whole comeback in it. "But it's the one with the veto you're scared of."

Gigi came through with his practice gear folded over her arm — the clean shell, the socks rolled the way the equipment room rolled them — and set it on the bench at his elbow, and Jacob, mid-wrap, with his hands full of tape and his season in his lap, did the thing the decent ones did: he noticed the staff had a logistics problem before she had to say so, and hooked the bench's spare stool out with his good foot so she could set the load down instead of holding it.
"You're the only one doesn't do the voice," he said.
"What voice."

"The—" He pitched his head to the side and made his voice soft and tragic, a fair imitation of every concerned adult in the building. "'How are we feeling about the ankle today, Jacob.' Like it's a pet that might die." He tore the tape with his teeth. "You just bring the towels. I respect the towels."
"Someone's got to respect them," Gigi said. "They're the only ones here doing their whole job."

He laughed — startled, real, the sound banging off the tile — and the trainer, clipboard and all, paused at a comeback he hadn't had to manufacture, and Gigi took her empty arms and her knowledge of the med room's second shelf back down the corridor, with his laugh still in the walls behind her, to do the rest of her shift.
