"I want to fold like a lawn chair," the kid said, and Jacob laughed — startled, real, the sound banging off the field-house wall the way it used to bang off the training-room tile — and finished the wrap and sent the boy off taped like a parcel, and turned to the next pilgrim with the patience of a man who had found, in the wreckage of his season, the one job in the building nobody could depth-chart him out of.

Gigi watched him from the water station with her hands in the cups and did the entry she had been doing since March, in the column that had no heading: a boy whose future she had edited with four minutes and a counting tray, teaching children to tape ankles, holding court, being whole in every way that remained available to him. He was not a symbol. He was not a lesson. He was a person with a mother who drove in from two counties away and a laugh that carried across a field, and the season she had taken from him sat in the middle of the charity morning like a stone in a shoe, and she walked on it, the way she walked on everything, without limping where anyone could see.

The shirt had been its own negotiation at six that morning, in the dorm, in front of the staff-grade mirror. The volunteer's shirts ran honest, which was more than could be said for the gala uniform, and the one with her name on the assignment sheet had been cut for the girl she had been in February. She had traded it — sideways, with a favor instead of a reason, the way staff traded everything — to a senior from the field crew who wore hers like a shrug, and the replacement hung a degree looser and tied a degree lower, and Pest, eating dry cereal out of the box at the desk that was also a table, had watched the whole transaction without comment, which was Pest's loudest register.
"Apron strings," Pest said at last, mildly, into the cereal.
"It's a shirt," Gigi said.
"Sure it is," Pest said. "File it how you want. The paperwork's already moving."

Week seventeen, and the rumor her clothes were keeping had started to need management the way everything in her life needed management: not solved, not confessed — administered. A looser shirt. A lower tie. A route map redrawn around the rooms with mirrors. She filed the morning under the term she had accepted in April: covered, while invisible, at a price that compounded daily, and went down to the field to be furniture at a charity event with her father's name on the banner over the gate.

At the cheer station, twenty feet of shade away, Layna Morris got down at kid height in the weak-tea shirt and taught a gap-toothed girl of maybe eight the opening counts of a routine, with a patience that had no camera anywhere near it and no audience but the girl's mother, standing at the rope with her hand over her mouth. The girl got it wrong twice. Layna got it wrong with her the third time, on purpose, at full commitment, and the girl's shriek of correction went up like a flare, and Layna — the announcement, the seating chart's first entry, the approved future of the Kreave line — sat down in the grass in her white shoes and laughed until the girl had to help her up. Gigi stood at the water jug with a cup in each hand and added the item to the folder that was getting complicated, next to the folded newspaper, next to the gala: the approved girl kept failing to audition for the villain's part, and she was doing it now in broad daylight, in grass stains, with an eight-year-old pulling her to her feet like a rope.

Across the field, on schedule, the kingdom produced its photograph: Blake at the passing station, down on one knee in the grass so the smallest boy could reach the throw, the boosters' cameras out, the announced couple's geometry assembling itself the way it assembled everywhere — Layna crossing to his side for the shot, her hand finding his arm at the practiced place, both of them lit and patient and entirely fluent. And for one second — the unit her whole life was denominated in — Blake's eyes came up off the cameras and crossed the field and found the water station, found her, the way they had found her in a tunnel in February, like the field had exactly one door in it.

She looked away first. That was new too, and they both knew it, and the looking away was its own entry: since the locker room, since the blood and the half-second of settlement he had read off her face like a headline, the discipline had acquired a second author. He protected her now by not looking. She protected herself by not being looked at. The arrangement had management on both sides, and the management was indistinguishable, from the field's edge, from loss.

The morning ran on rails of sunshine and logistics. Kids rotated. Water cups emptied and refilled. At the passing station Blake performed the kingdom's favorite miracle on schedule — a famous boy being patient with small boys, his public gentleness running like a metronome — and the cameras the boosters had brought found him the way cameras always found him, and Layna, beside Gigi, watched him be found with an expression Gigi had never seen on her in the light: not pride, not performance. Assessment. The look of a woman reading a document she had been handed at birth and was finally old enough to check the math on.

"You know what nobody tells you about being the announcement?" Layna said, in the lull, handing a cup to a kid without looking at the cup, her eyes still on the field. "You don't get told. I found out I was Blake Kreave's girlfriend from a seating chart. I was twelve. It came with a program." She said it the way other people said the weather. "There's a photograph of the two of us at that dinner. I keep it in my room. Not because it's us. Because it's the only picture I have where I can see the exact minute it happened — where I'm smiling and I don't know yet."
Gigi's hands went on filling cups, because hands were trained and hers had never once required her permission.
"Do you love him?" she said, and heard herself say it — the staff ghost, asking the queen a question with no staff grammar in it at all — and could not call it back, and did not entirely want to.

Layna looked at her then, properly, the way she had looked at the booster at the gala: with the whole intelligence on. For one second the water station stood at the edge of something with no name in either of their vocabularies — and then Layna smiled, and the smile was tired and real and entirely unbothered, and she answered like a woman answering a question she asked herself on a schedule.

"I love the version of my life where this makes sense," she said. "Blake's just the most expensive part of it." She picked up the next cup. "You have the only honest face at this school, Gavin. Do you know that? Everybody else is posing for a photograph that hasn't been taken yet. You're the only one who ever looks like you're somewhere."

It was at that moment — in the middle of Layna's sentence, in the middle of the queen's one unguarded paragraph, with the sun standing on the field and the kids' noise running around them like weather — that the child moved.

episodes.title: Eleven Feet
paras: Not a pain. Not the nausea, not the flutters her body had been filing under digestion for weeks, the body's small print. A knock, from inside, deliberate as a knuckle on a door: once, low, and unmistakably not hers. Seventeen weeks of arithmetic stood up in her all at once and became a person with timing. The cup in her hand stayed level — she would be proud of that later, in the dark, in the ledger; the cup stayed level and her face did not change — and the whole architecture of the secret rearranged itself around the fact that the secret had just announced itself to the only audience it had: her.
"You okay?" Layna said. "You look like you saw weather."
"Stood up too fast," Gigi said. "Sun's doing audits today."

"Then sit before you fall, staff," Layna said, and kicked the crate out with her foot the way Jacob had kicked a stool out in March with his good one, and Gigi sat on the equipment crate at the edge of the frame with the water jug sweating beside her and her hand flat on the crate's edge, an inch from where it wanted to be, and under her apron — under the weak-tea shirt, under the whole costume of the facilities — the knock came again, smaller, experimental, a second opinion: there. And there. A person, testing the walls of the only room they'd ever had, in the middle of the announced girl's sentence, in broad daylight, at a charity event, in a town whose every wall had somebody's father's name on it.

She did not put her hand where it wanted to go. That discipline cost more than the med room had. She sat on the crate and breathed and smiled at the queen with the face Layna had just called the only honest one at the school, and the honesty of it was this: she was having the most important moment of her life in public, at a water station, and the only witness was the woman the world believed it belonged to.

Layna was called away then — the squad's photograph, the ribbon rehearsal, the announcement's other duties — and the shade tent emptied into sunshine, and Misty arrived from the concession side with two lemonades and the expression of a woman who had been watching a station for an hour and had composed a review.

"Democracy update," Misty said, handing her a cup. "The queen does manual labor now. Jacob's a pediatrician. The king's been tackled by a seven-year-old and the seven-year-old's telling it at school Monday like a war story." She sat on the crate's other end. "Meanwhile the staff's finest stands here getting sunburned in a shirt somebody else got assigned. We have got to unionize, Gavin. I'm serious. I did the math on a napkin. The napkin cried."
"Eat your lemonade," Gigi said.

"Drinking it. It's a beverage. You eat when the bug allows." Misty squinted at her across the crate. "You look like a ghost at a christening today. That's an upgrade from the wedding, I guess. Progress."

Under the weak-tea shirt, low and deliberate, the knock came a third time — not for an audience now, not timed to anyone's sentence. Just there. A person, keeping their own hours, in the only room they'd ever had, while the staff's finest sat on a crate drinking lemonade and being filed under weather by her best friend. Gigi put her hand down flat on the crate between them, an inch from its new address, and drank the lemonade, and said nothing, and the nothing — for once, in all the months of nothings she had furnished and filed and spent — was not a strategy. It was just a girl on a crate, in the sun, keeping the first appointment her child had ever made with her, in the only company she had.
The photo-op assembled at midday with the inevitability of weather.

The Mayor came down the field in a cluster of staff and lenses, shaking the hands the cameras liked, with the ribbon stretched between two posts at midfield and the scissors riding on a cushion like a relic of the state. He was shorter than the arena screen made him and more ordinary, a man in a good suit doing the job his face had been elected to do, and the crowd performed its side of the liturgy beautifully: applause at the practiced places, laughter invested in advance, the whole town reading from the same seating chart. Gigi worked the edge of it with a crate of water cups, restocking the station the camera line had displaced, moving at furniture speed along the exact border of the frame — near enough to be in the photograph, which she would be, a blurred girl at the margin with a crate in her arms, and far enough to be out of its caption, which she also would be, because captions were written for the announced.

She counted the distance the way she counted everything, because counting was what her hands did when her heart was busy. From the crate to the ribbon: eleven feet. Eleven feet of May sunshine between the city's most visible man and the girl he had never once looked at, while his grandchild knocked, experimentally, from inside the girl's body, at the volume of a secret. The cameras went off like a volley. He smiled the smile that twenty years of rooms like this had engraved, cut the ribbon at the mark, and held the scissors up for the lenses, and Gigi — carrying water past the edge of the official record of the day he came to her workplace and smiled for the future of the city's children — understood that the erasure did not even require his attention anymore. It ran on rails, like the charity day, like the calendar, like her own body. It was the most efficient machine in Bridge Water, and she was staff to it, and the cups needed refilling, and she refilled them.

She never got closer than eleven feet. The number went into the ledger that night without commentary, because some entries were only numbers, the way some distances were only ever going to be measured by the person standing at the wrong end of them.
The opportunity to climb came in the afternoon, dressed as nothing, the way the real ones always did.

The event was thinning. Priest was working the field's edge with his notebook, collecting the day for the paper — the mayor, the ribbon, the famous boy being patient with small boys — and he stopped at the water station in the shade's last hour with the calm of a man who took dictation at executions, and he said, to the air, to the cups, to the staff ghost he had been professionally not-noticing since February: "Slow news week, Gavin. Kingdom Cracking needs a fourth installment and the kingdom's being photogenic at me." He turned a page he didn't write on. "You hear confession long enough, you stop needing names. The sins have handwriting."

In March she would have audited the contents of her pockets for something to feed him — a true thing, harmless, precisely placed, the machine's next meal. She had one in her pocket today that would have bought the whole summer: the queen, off duty, at a water station, saying out loud that her whole life had been seated beside a boy when she was twelve and she wasn't sure love was the word the program used. It was true. It was harmless, by the standards of everything else she had ever spent. It would have cracked the announcement's shine from the inside, in the approved girl's own voice, and it cost nothing but timing.
She handed Priest a cup of water.
"Hydrate," she said. "Confession's thirsty work."

He looked at the cup, and then at her, with the first genuinely surprised expression she had ever put on his face, and he drank the water, and he wrote nothing down, and the machine went hungry for one more day. She stood in the thinning light with her hand finally, finally allowed to rest where it wanted — low, flat, against the weak-tea shirt, while the last kids were collected and the banners started coming down — and she filed the refusal where she filed the things that were not rungs: beside the folded schedule in her locker she would find in June and not throw away, in the drawer of decisions that were also data. The day the child kicked was the day she didn't climb. She couldn't have said whether it was mercy, or strategy, or the simple arithmetic of a girl whose hands were suddenly full. She only knew the ladder had stood there all afternoon with its next rung at eye level, and her feet had stayed on the ground, and the ground, for once, had felt less like losing.
That night, in the dorm, with Pest asleep above her and the radiator silent for the season, she did the books by lamplight with one hand still learning its new address.

The envelope: two hundred and nineteen dollars — two hundred and five, and fourteen more folded out of a week's café tips, smoothed flat, tucked in like they were being put to bed by somebody who loved them. A hundred and forty of it still earmarked for the door across town. The rest of it a future, at retail, one small bill at a time. She wrote the week's number in the margin — 17, small and clean — and underneath, in the second column, in the body's own categories, she wrote the entry twice before it satisfied her, because the body had apparently expanded its vocabulary and the ledger was going to have to expand with it:
Moved: from the inside. Not mine. On its own schedule. Eleven feet: the whole distance. Hands: full.

She closed the notebook and lay in the dark with her hand resting where it rested now, by default, the way it had started resting in February like it had its own opinions, and she thought about the queen's tired, honest laugh, and about a knock, low and deliberate, delivered in the middle of the wrong girl's sentence — hello, in the only language the child had, at the one person it had been addressed to all along.
How do you hate the girl in the photograph, when your child just kicked hello in the middle of her sentence?

episodes.title: Managed
paras: Week eighteen arrived with its paperwork in order and its patience finished.

The body had stopped negotiating in private. That was the difference May made: what March had filed as rumor, May was entering as fact, in a hand that got steadier every week. The shirts had been traded twice now. The apron strings Pest had joked about in the dorm had begun, quietly, to file their report — not to any eye that wasn't already reading her, not yet, but the geometry of Gigi Gavin in a uniform had acquired an editor, and the editor was not her. She redrew her routes around the rooms with mirrors. She carried the cart at the angle staff carried carts, which hid more than any garment could. She did the arithmetic of doorways the way she had done it since she was six years old, in houses where being read correctly was the first step toward being handled: exits, two; witnesses, none that counted; the width of the remaining invisibility, measured in weeks, in a margin, in a small clean hand.

Eighteen. The notebook's margin said it without decoration. Eighteen weeks since a championship night in December, eighteen weeks of a secret that had begun as a plastic stick in a staff bathroom and had become, by slow administrative stages, the governing document of her life.
And the secret had acquired a second accountant. That was the spring's other weather, and it frightened her more than the shirts did: Blake was keeping count.

Not of the pregnancy — he believed there wasn't one; that was the whole architecture — but of her. Since the locker room, since the blood on the tiles and the half-second of settlement he had read off her face like a headline, the king had begun a quiet census of the staff ghost: where she was standing before things happened. She read it in the small print of his behavior the way she read everything, completely. He was in the training-room corridor on Tuesdays and Fridays now — not entering the med room, never entering it, just present at an hour that used to be hers alone, with an errand that never quite explained itself. He had asked Franky nothing and the equipment manager one thing — her rotation, dressed up as a question about towel counts. He looked at her hands once, at load-out, the way a man looks at evidence he is not yet willing to log. He was protecting her, the way she had understood in the locker room that he would: actively, silently, at compound interest. But protection, in a boy raised by a seating chart, took the shape of surveillance, and she could feel the net of it tightening by a thread a week, and she understood, with the clarity that visited her in steam, that his count and her body's count were running toward the same date from opposite directions, and that the date was not hers to choose anymore.

Pest had said it in April, in the dorm, with the radiator making its one argument: I cover while it's invisible. The term had a second clause, which Pest, being Pest, had not needed to state: and the week it stops being invisible, Gavin, the telling stops being your idea and becomes the weather's.
It became the weather on a Tuesday, at the café, at the kingdom's lunch hour, with the grill going and the squad's table in the light.

Pest was working the register end of the line that week — the café handoff had become one of her stations the way the dawn rounds had, exactly, dryly, with the air of a woman keeping a tab in a book nobody had shown her yet. The team came through in their warm-ups with their trays and their noise, and Blake came through with them, and performed the whole liturgy of his public life in the space of one transaction: the captain's ease, the joke for the freshman, the card out of the wallet without looking. Pest took the card. Pest ran the card. And Pest, who had read the margins in a laundry locker and priced a constitution out of them and waited five weeks for a telling that had not come, looked at the most announced boy in the state and spent her precision exactly once, in the flat professional voice of a woman confirming an order:
"Eighteen weeks, Kreave. In case anybody's still counting stomach bugs."

The line moved on. The tray slid. Whatever Blake Kreave's face did with the number happened behind the performance, which reasserted itself the way it always did, on schedule, like weather changing back. But Gigi — sliding to the cold line with her jaw set against the grill's perfume, three stations away — saw his hand stop, once, on the counter's edge, the way a listener stops. All at once. With the pencil already still.

She did not hear the sentence. She didn't need to. She knew the register's whole vocabulary, and she knew what a number sounded like when it landed on the one person in the building whose arithmetic it completed. Pest caught her eye across the line, once, without apology and without triumph, the way a clerk stamps a document she intends to honor, and went back to the register, and the lunch hour closed over all three of them like water.

"He counts from December," Pest said that night, in the dorm, before Gigi could build the question. "I watched him do it at the register. You could see the months come off his face like pages." She climbed into the top bunk with her textbook like a shield. "My cover ends when it shows, Gavin. It's showing to exactly one person now, and he's the author. That was the invoice in April. Today I just delivered it."
"I was going to tell him," Gigi said.

"You've been going to tell him since February," Pest said, from the dark, not unkindly, which was the part that made it unanswerable. "It's the longest commute in this building. The body was going to beat you to the announcement by about a week. I just made sure the announcement had a return address." A page turned. "Whatever he does with arithmetic is his religion's problem now."
Blake Kreave did arithmetic the way his family did everything: completely, privately, and in the direction of a payment.

Eighteen weeks from the middle of December was not a difficult sum, and it was not a sum a man could arrive at and then unknow: it meant the February question — did you handle it — had been answered by a silence he had furnished himself, and that the furnishing had been the whole of it, and that everything he had done inside the furnished belief (the sleep, the relief, the restored shoulders, the extra reps taken on a clear conscience off a cart in a tunnel) had been done in a house with a heartbeat in the walls. He did not come to the equipment room that night. He did something more Kreave than that, something older, something his father's religion had taught him before it taught him to read: he went to close the account.

The good clinic across town — the one he had named in February, in the steam, with such desperate fluency: the good one, not the campus one — kept ordinary hours and an unremarkable door on a street off Bridge Water Avenue, and on Wednesday afternoon the kingdom's golden boy stood at its front desk in his warm-ups with his wallet in his hand, performing the only sacrament he had ever been taught for a thing this size.

He wanted to settle whatever was outstanding. He wanted to confirm that a bill from February or March — an appointment, a procedure, the labs — had been paid in full, and to pay any remainder himself, and to close it. The receptionist, who had the kind, wall-like professionalism of a woman who had been asked every version of this question by every version of this boy, gave him the whole of what the law and the clinic's cheerful typeface allowed: nothing. She could not confirm or share anything about anyone. There was nothing a third party could settle. If he was a patient, she could help him; if he was not, the desk had reached the end of its road.

He stood there with the preparedness in his hand — the envelope religion, arriving two months late at a desk that did not accept it — and understood, perhaps for the first time in his life, that there existed a room in his own town where his name was not a currency and his money was not an argument. He thanked her. He was gentle about it; gentleness was the one coin he minted himself. He put the wallet away. He walked out of the good clinic across town into the May sunshine, with the number eighteen still counting itself in the back of his mind and nowhere in the world to spend it —

— and Gigi Gavin came up the clinic's steps with her coat over her arm and a folded leaflet in her hand, on an errand she had scheduled that morning with her whole chest: to book, in person, at last, the appointment she had not booked in eighteen weeks of crossing this door in every way except through it.

They stood on the steps of the one address in Bridge Water neither of them could explain, in daylight, in May, with the street going past at errand speed, and looked at each other the way people look at weather arriving off a clear sky.

His face did three things. She had been keeping that face's whole repertoire since February and she read the three things the way she read a margin — but the order was wrong this time, the season's order, inverted: not happiness, not gentleness. Recognition first, entire and unguarded, the boy who had been counting a staff ghost's whereabouts for six weeks arriving at the sum of her. Then the ghost of February — she watched his own relief come back to him from across three months and be recognized, and die of the recognition, standing up. And then the fury arrived, exactly on schedule, and it was not the fury of a boy who had been lied to. It was the fury of a boy who had been managed, and who knew the management's whole floor plan because he had been raised inside the firm that invented it.
"You never went," he said.

episodes.title: Locked From Inside
paras: It was not loud. Nothing about Blake Kreave was ever loud in the places that mattered; that was the breeding, and the breeding held even here, on the steps, with the future standing in front of him in a traded shirt at week eighteen. He looked at her — really looked, at doorway distance, in daylight, at a body in its own clothes with no uniform geometry left to negotiate with — and the body said the rest of it for her, the way bodies did now, at conversational volume, to anyone who had ever known it in the dark.
"I went past it," Gigi said. "Every week since February. I know its hours better than the staff do. I just never went in."
"You let me—" He stopped. The sentence had too many true endings and he was choosing among them like a man at a ledge. "At the brunch. I texted you. You let me hear that as a yes."

"I let you hear what you needed," she said. "You did the rest at home, Blake. You furnished it. I just never corrected the hearing." She held the leaflet in her hand like a bookmark in an argument. "I was coming in today. That's the part nobody's managing. I was coming in today, on my own schedule, with my own money — and then you were going to get the whole document, from me, in a room, like a person. That was the plan. It wasn't a good plan. It was the only one that didn't have your father's calendar in it. And now the weather's told you first, so—" She looked at the clinic door, and at him, and at the street performing its innocence around the two of them. "Not here."
"Where."

"Load-out," she said. "Seven. The room where you're a person." She went up the steps past him — past the author of it, standing in the sunshine with his wallet full of a currency the desk had declined — and through the door she had crossed in every way except this one for eighteen weeks, and she booked the appointment at the desk inside with her own name and her own voice, at conversational volume, while he stood outside in the light being the kingdom's most expensive piece of furniture.
The equipment room at seven had the day's last steam in it and the towels stacked like a held breath.

He came down the tunnel the way he always came — out of the last of the performance, jacket over his shoulders — and he closed the door, which he had never done, and the room became the only room in the building with the whole truth in it, and he stood in it with his back to the shelving and said the thing he had apparently been composing since the steps:
"You ran me."

"No. Let me get the whole document out, since documents are the religion now." His voice stayed down. It stayed gentle, which was worse. "February, I ask you if you handled it, and you send me silence, and I build a house in it. I sleep, Gigi. Do you understand that? I slept like it was my job. I told Franky we're fine in a tunnel in front of your cart. I took Jacob's reps — Jacob's, off his ankle, off your—" The sentence broke there and was rebuilt by hand. "I took them on a clear conscience. I stood in a locker room in April and watched you enjoy what you did to two of my friends and I protected you, I kept the count and I said nothing, and the whole time I was protecting—" He looked at her stomach, once, the way you look at a document you've been handed in a language you half-read. "You managed me like staff, Gavin. You scheduled my ignorance. You decided what I could carry and when I could carry it and you ran the whole arrangement out of a laundry locker at a profit. My father couldn't have done it cleaner."
She let the room have that, because most of it was true and the true part deserved its full width.

"Your father," she said, "invented it. I just have the accent." She set the towel down she had been holding like a passport. "You want the document, Blake? Here's the document. In February you asked me one question, in a text, with no punctuation, from a hallway at a booster party — did you handle it — and you know what you were asking. You weren't asking about me. You were asking whether the calendar was safe. And I didn't answer, and you heard yes, because yes was the only answer your whole life had ever filed under a girl's silence. I didn't forge that hearing. You brought it with you, pre-installed, like the envelope."
"The envelope—"

"Is in my locker," she said. "Behind the towels. Unopened. Unspent. Every dollar of your father's preparedness, sitting in the dark since February, in a building where I count other people's money for a living. You want to talk about being managed? I managed one thing, Blake. I managed not to be purchased. You paid me to disappear. I just did it my way."
The room went very quiet, the steam's quiet, the held-breath quiet of towels.

Then the questions came out of him the way they should have come out in February — not the calendar's questions, hers. Had she seen a doctor. Had anyone, in eighteen weeks, so much as taken her pulse. "The leaflet," she said. "The margins. Pest with a sandwich. That's the medical establishment, Blake. It's been very thorough." The vitamins — "Fourteen dollars. February. My envelope, not yours." Sleep — she looked at him then, and let him do that arithmetic himself, the dawn rounds and the cot and the arm over her eyes in the staff room dark, all the stolen eleven minutes of it, and she watched the captain of two sports understand that while he had been sleeping like it was his job, the mother of his child had been napping in uniform between loads. He sat down, finally, on the shelving's edge, among the towels, in the posture of a man whose legs had filed a report of their own, and the sitting was its own paragraph in the document: the king, in a laundry, at eye level with the staff, reading the file in full at last.

"You should have told me," he said, and the fury had burned down by then into the thing underneath it, which was older and had his real voice in it. "Whatever I did with it. However I failed it. You should have let me fail it knowing."

"Yes," Gigi said. "I should have. Write it in the margin. I kept it because telling you meant your father's calendar got a vote, and I have been outvoted by that calendar in every room I've ever stood in, and I was not — I was not going to watch it happen to this too. That's not a defense. It's just the paperwork." She picked up the towel again because her hands needed the job. "I carried it alone for eighteen weeks. That part I'd do again. The part where you slept — Blake, that's yours. I let you. But I didn't make it comfortable. You did that part at home."

He looked at her for a long time then, with the three things finally settled into one thing, and the one thing was the expression of a man reading a document in full for the first time and finding his own signature already on it, in February, in a hallway, in the grammar of an unanswered text.
"How far," he said quietly.

"Eighteen weeks. I counted on your steps today, so you know the margin's honest." She folded the towel, once, correctly. "The clinic's booked now. Next Friday. Under my name. The whole of it under my name — that part was never negotiable, and it still isn't."
"And the money for it—"

"Costs a hundred and forty dollars, which I have, in an envelope of my own, that I earned in smiles I didn't mean. Not his. Mine. That was the whole point of the arithmetic since February, and I am not revising it tonight."

He absorbed that the way he absorbed play calls, entire and without flinching, and she watched him arrive — slowly, the way weather arrives off water — at the door the whole hour had been building toward. It stood open in front of him, and everything she knew about Blake Kreave said he would walk out of it into the announced part of his evening and let the machinery of his life re-price the problem by morning. He had always gone. He had never once stayed past the point where the kingdom started asking where he was.
"We tell no one," he said. "Not yet."

She heard the sentence arrive in its February grammar and stand in the room in a new key, and she understood, standing there with the towel in her hands, that the words had crossed over: not yet was no longer a postponement performed on her. It was a lock being turned from the inside of a cage by a man walking into it voluntarily — the cage door closing, this time, with him inside it, on her side of the wall.
"Blake—"

"I'm not asking," he said, and the gentleness was back, and it was not the gentleness of the envelope this time; it was the gentleness of a decision, which she had never heard from him before and did not yet know how to file. "I'm telling you the terms of my own—" He stopped, and rebuilt it, honestly, the way men in his family never rebuilt anything. "I don't know what I am in this yet. I know I'm not the man who walks out of this room and lets the calendar have it. Not this time. We figure out what it costs. In here. Where I'm a person."
She did the books that night in the dorm with Pest asleep above her and the radiator resuming its one argument for the last weeks of spring.

The envelope: two hundred and thirty-one dollars — two hundred and nineteen, and twelve more from a week of café tips and one booster who tipped like he was apologizing for the century. All of it hers. All of it counted. A hundred and forty of it spoken for since February, by a door she had finally walked through, at a desk, in her own name. She wrote the week's number in the margin — 18, small and clean — and beneath it, in the second column, in the body's own categories, the entry took three attempts, because the categories had a new resident and the ledger was going to have to expand again:
Told: everything, out loud, in a room. Kept: everything. The difference: there isn't one anymore — there's just two people carrying it.
She closed the notebook and lay in the dark listening to the building settle, and thought about a sentence that had locked a door from the inside, and about whose hand had been on the key this time.
When the lie you've been living inside finally opens its door, why does the man walk in — and lock it behind him?

episodes.title: Terms
paras: The negotiated secret had a shape by the end of its first week, and the shape was a treaty, and like every treaty in history it was mostly a list of things two exhausted parties agreed to stop doing in public.

They drafted it the way they did everything: in the equipment room, at load-out, in the hour when the building belonged to the staff and the boy was a person. He brought the terms the way he brought everything new — all at once, overprepared, a man who had been doing arithmetic for three days and had arrived with a structure.

"The clinic bills me," he said. "Direct. Card on file, invoices to my phone, no—" He stopped himself, because the word had become an exhibit in their house. "No cash. Nothing through your hands that you have to carry. You book what you need, when you need it. The desk already has my—"
"No."
"Gigi—"

"My name books it. My name attends it. Your money arrives the way weather arrives, Blake — usefully, and from a distance, and without a ceremony." She counted towels while she talked, because the treaty went easier with the job running underneath it. "And his money stays in my locker."

He looked at the locker. It stood at the room's end with its dent shaped like somebody's old frustration, behind the spare uniform, holding the thickest silence in the building: his father's envelope, unopened since February, untouched by the arithmetic that had just reorganized both their lives.
"That's still the law," he said. It wasn't a question, and she heard him file it as one anyway.

"That's still the law. It sits there until September. Then I hand it back to you in the room where you gave it to me, or it buys something that isn't an erasure, and either way it ends the way it began: unopened. That's not a negotiation point. That's a load-bearing wall."
There was one more article, and she saved it for when the counting was done, because it was the one that changed his posture.

"Pest knows," she said. "Has known since April. She read the margins in my locker — the count, the second column, all of it. She covers my dawn rounds and my supervisors' questions, and her cover has a term on it: it runs while it's invisible. The day it shows, she's out, and she's out because her own file is two strikes deep and the secret would point at her paperwork first. So the treaty has a third citizen, Blake. She's unwilling, she's expensive, and she's the only reason there was a secret left for you to walk into."
He absorbed that the way he absorbed everything that spring, standing still, at full price. "The roommate."

"The roommate. The one person in this building who looked at the evidence and priced it correctly in one sitting, which puts her ahead of both of us." She watched him do the new arithmetic — the secret's census rising by one, the surface area doubling in his face. "She doesn't want your money either. She wants you told and the telling done, and as of Tuesday she considers her invoice paid. What she thinks of you is not in my department. I believe the phrase was a boy who sleeps."
"And now?"
"Now you don't," she said. "That's the whole of her diplomacy. Don't make her revise it."
"What do I get," he said, and the question came out rawer than he intended it to, "in the treaty. For the money. For the silence. What do I actually get, Gigi."

"The count," she said. "The dates. The truth in a room, at conversational volume, when there's truth to have. You get to stop being managed." She set the last stack down in its order. "You don't get a vote on the paperwork. You don't get a say in the delivery room's seating chart, not yet, not in May. And you don't get to look at me in tunnels. That one's not cruelty, Blake. That's load-bearing too. The day your eyes change in public is the day Steff starts a file, and her files don't close."
He absorbed the terms the way he absorbed play calls, entire and without flinching, and she watched the captain in him do the thing the captain always did: he started drilling the new formation.
"Friday," he said. "Four o'clock. I drive you."
"You wait in the car," she said. "Across the street. The room is mine."

"The room is yours," he agreed, and wrote nothing down, because nothing in the treaty was ever going to be written down anywhere but a margin, and they both knew the margin's address by heart. "What's the count."
"Nineteen on Tuesday."

"Nineteen," he repeated, the way a man memorizes a country he intends to be able to find in the dark. The good clinic across town, on Friday, at four o'clock, had a waiting room with chairs that matched and a door that closed, and Gigi Gavin sat in it in her own name for the first time in her life and listened to a building make only the sounds of competence.

The paperwork said GAVIN, GIGI in the clean typeface of an institution that had never once needed her to be furniture. The forms asked their questions in order. She answered them in her own voice, at conversational volume, in a room where no one was performing: the dates, the count, the history she could give and the history she couldn't, all of it entered in a file with her name spelled right on it. It was the least dramatic hour of her entire spring, and it undid her more completely than the locker room had: nineteen weeks of managing a fact alone, in margins and traded shirts and route maps drawn around mirrors — and here it was being carried by a system, in the open, by professionals, as though it were the most ordinary weather in the world. As though girls were allowed to simply have it attended to.

The clinician had gray in her hair and the flat kindness of a woman who had delivered every version of this news in every register it came in. She measured. She confirmed. She said the word nineteen like it was a fact and not a verdict, and then she said the thing Gigi had been bracing for since February, in the mildest voice in the building:

"First visit at nineteen weeks. We'll catch everything up — bloods, measurements, the picture. It happens more than you'd think, arriving here by the scenic route. What matters is you're in the system now."

In the system. On paper. Under her own name, spelled right. Gigi sat on the papered table with her hands folded in her lap like a girl at a recital and understood that some part of her had been waiting to be scolded — had budgeted for the scolding, had priced it into every week of the walk past the door — and that the absence of it was the most expensive thing the clinic had yet handed her, because it could not be folded, or filed, or refused. It could only be had.
Then the clinician turned the speaker on.

The heartbeat came out of the machine the way everything real had ever come to her: sideways, at low volume, and undeniable — a fast, wet, galloping rhythm, nothing like the stately count she had been keeping in margins, a stranger's tempo entirely, a person keeping their own hours at a speed that made her whole spring look slow. Her hand went to the table's edge. Her other hand — the traitor, the one with its own opinions, the one that had started resting low on her stomach in the dark in February — stayed exactly where it was, flat over the fact, as if it had known the frequency all along and was only now being proven right in public.
"There," the clinician said, with professional satisfaction, the way you confirmed weather. "That's the whole orchestra."

Gigi laughed. It startled her more than the sound had — a real laugh, the corridor kind, in a clinic room, at week nineteen, with her name on the door and the orchestra playing — and the laugh had something in it she did not trust at all, something with no column in any ledger she kept, and she filed it where she filed the things that were not rungs and not costs: beside the folded schedule, in the drawer of decisions that were also data. Hope. Blooming, against her will, at conversational volume, in a room with a door that closed.

The desk, on her way out, was kind in the typeface way: the visit was a hundred and forty dollars, the constant, the wall that had been a door since April — and it had been taken care of. The receptionist said it with the pleasure of a woman delivering simplicity: a card on file, a confirmation already sent, nothing owed, nothing to sign. Gigi stood at the desk with her file under her arm and priced what it cost her to let a thing be taken care of — the exact weight of it, which was the weight of a wall becoming a door she'd had no hand in opening — and paid it, because the alternative was the arithmetic of February, and she was done letting February set her prices.

The printout came in two copies without her asking, the gray blur of the orchestra's first photograph, a profile like a weather map of a country she was going to live in. She put one in the notebook, in the back, where the leaflet used to live. The other one she carried out into the May light folded in her palm, already knowing its destination, already composing the warning that would fail to govern it.

episodes.title: The Medical File
paras: He was across the street in the car, where the treaty put him, with the engine off and his hands at ten and two on a wheel that wasn't going anywhere, like a man holding a formation after the whistle.

She crossed Bridge Water Avenue in the late light with the file under her arm and got into the passenger seat of the kingdom's most photographed car like she was boarding a vehicle she had every right to, and for one whole minute neither of them performed anything at all. Then he looked at the file, and at her, and his face did the February three things in the new order — no terror this time; the terror had been spent in April, on steps, in stages — happiness arriving unguarded and staying a full second too long, and then the gentleness, which was becoming something else now, something with a spine in it.
"Well," he said.

"Nineteen weeks," she said. "Measured, not estimated. Bloods taken. Everything caught up or catching." She opened her palm, where the second printout had gone soft at the folds from being carried like evidence. "That's the whole orchestra."

He took it the way he had taken the plastic stick in February — like a bird with a broken wing — and looked at the gray weather of it for a long time, in the parked car, in the ordinary light, with the clinic's door closed behind them and the whole announced world nine blocks and one universe away.
"Don't keep it anywhere stupid," she said.
"I won't."

"You will," she said, without heat, because she knew his religion's whole liturgy of keeping. "Keep it somewhere stupid on a schedule I can't audit, then. Lockers get opened, Blake. Bags get searched the day somebody's looking for something else entirely. I'm giving it to you because the treaty says the truth in a room — and I'm telling you its price while I hand it over, because that's the treaty's other half."

"I hear you," he said, and folded it — carefully, once, the way you folded things that mattered — and put it in the inside pocket of his jacket, over his heart, where a photograph of him carrying it would have been worth more than the building. "What's it—" He stopped. Rebuilt it. "What did they say it needs. The— orchestra. What do I do."
"You're doing it," she said, surprising them both. "Apparently this is the job now. Showing up with a card and a car and no envelope."

He laughed then — the real one, the corridor one, the one that was only ever hers — and drove her back across the avenue's whole length in the blue May evening, past the gates, past the arena standing enormous over its kingdom, and dropped her at the service entrance because that was the door her life used, and the treaty held, and neither of them said the thing that the heartbeat had made available in the car like a third passenger. Hope was riding with them now, uninvited and unbilled, and they were both too well trained to look directly at it. Franky had been keeping his own count since April, and unlike Blake's, Franky's count had a theory in it.

Franky was the bomb with a heartbeat: he loved Blake Kreave the way dogs and brothers and best friends loved, which was by following. He had seen the king stand at a shut equipment-room door in March, checking whether a house he used to live in still had his key in the lock. He had seen the count-keeping begin in April — the corridor appearances, the question to the equipment manager dressed as towels. He had seen the locker room, and what Blake had not said in it, and had filed that too, in the loyal, unexamined archive of a boy whose whole faith was that his best friend's silences were a country he was expected to guard without a map.
On Friday he followed the car.

It was not malice and it was not suspicion; it was devotion, doing what devotion did when it was given no instructions. He followed at a distance his conscience could defend, in his own truck, across Bridge Water Avenue and over to the side of town where the clinics kept their unremarkable doors, and he sat in a lot across the street and watched the kingdom's golden boy wait in a parked car for the length of a medical appointment, alone, in May, when the program believed him to be at a film review that did not exist.

He did not see Gigi. She had come by bus and gone in by the door the patients used while he was watching the car — the staff ghost's whole education, spent in one afternoon without her knowledge: she was invisible even to surveillance. What Franky saw was a star, a clinic, ninety minutes, and a stillness in his best friend that he had only ever seen after injuries — and Franky, who knew the kingdom's whole economy of the body, built the only theory the evidence could hold in the country he lived in: a hidden injury. A secret treatment. A star being managed off the books, in the spring of his draft year, with the program, the scouts, and the seating chart all uninformed.

A hidden injury was a five-alarm fact in the kingdom's arithmetic. It was also — and Franky felt this in his chest like a second heartbeat — the kind of fact a best friend had to get in front of, because stories like that didn't stay hidden, they leaked, and a leak with no management on it was how kingdoms fell. So he did the loyal thing, the disastrous thing, the thing the bomb with a heartbeat had been built by the whole spring to do: he went to the man who managed the kingdom's memory, to trade a question for a warning, off the record, between professionals.

"Hypothetically," Franky said, at the press table, in the emptying arena, while Priest typed with the calm of a man taking dictation at an execution. "If a certain crown was getting treated across town, and the program didn't know — that'd be the kind of thing a paper wouldn't just print, right? You'd sit on something like that. Ethically."
Priest's typing did not pause, which was how Franky knew he had the man's entire attention.

"Hypothetically," Priest said, "papers sit on all kinds of things. Papers are furniture with long memories." The keys kept their rhythm. "Is the crown's treatment the kind that heals, Franky? Or the kind that gets managed?"
"Managed," Franky said, miserably, loyal to the end. "Off the books. Ninety minutes, Friday, across town. That's not a sprain schedule."

"No," Priest agreed, and something in his voice was almost gentle. "It isn't." He turned a page in the notebook that lived beside the keyboard — the paper one, the real one — and wrote the quote down in the handwriting that never appeared in print, in the file that had been growing since February in the paper's smallest type: KINGDOM CRACKING, and under it, in the freshest ink in the building, a new chapter heading, in the grammar of a man who had just been handed a door and was in no hurry at all to open it: THE MEDICAL FILE.

Gigi heard the theory on Monday, in the café, in the staff's weather, at third hand and rising: the king was hiding an injury. A senior had it from a trainer's aide who had it from a laugh in the locker room — Kreave, treated in secret, across town, the program in the dark. She stood at the cold line with the cups in her hands and priced the wrong fact's terrible architecture: it had a clinic in it. It had a secrecy, a schedule, a payment made in May. It was the truth with its face turned ninety degrees, and it was more dangerous than the truth had ever been, because the truth could be denied in one voice, by two people, in a room — and the wrong fact was already out walking around in the kingdom's mouth, looking for the one detail that would turn its face the rest of the way.
Pest heard the theory on Tuesday, in the dorm, from Gigi herself, because the constitution ran both directions now and information was the rent the room charged.

"So the official story is his knee," Pest said, eating dry cereal out of the box at the desk that was also a table. "His kingdom thinks he's being treated for a secret injury. That's the firewall your boyfriend's best friend built you — a clinic with the wrong patient in it." She considered the architecture with professional respect. "It's almost good, Gavin. It's got his name on the door and yours on nothing. The problem with almost is it's a direction."
"He put it in Priest's file himself," Gigi said. "He thinks he's managing it."

"Of course he does. Loyalty's just secrecy with a press office." Pest set the box down. "Here's what I know about files, since files are my whole personality: a file with a clinic in it doesn't stay wrong forever. It stays wrong until somebody asks it one question it can't hold at ninety degrees. Then it turns, all at once, and everybody who ever posed for it is in the photograph." She climbed up to the top bunk with her textbook like a shield. "Cover continues, by the way. While invisible. Wanted that in the record. But your secret's got staff and a budget and a medical file now. It's not a secret anymore, Gavin. It's an administration. Administrations fall louder."

She wrote the week's number in the margin that night — 19, small and clean — and counted the envelope with hands that did their job a half-second behind her eyes: two hundred and forty dollars. Two hundred and thirty-one, and nine more from the week's tips. His father's envelope stood unopened in the locker behind her like a second spine, and Blake had begun looking at it, in treaty sessions, the way a man looks at a country he is no longer allowed to emigrate from.

Underneath the 19, in the second column, in the body's own categories, she wrote the entry for the new era, and it was not in any category the body had used before, because the body had never before kept its books with company:
Heard: it. On a speaker. At conversational volume. His: a card. A car. No envelope. New file: his name on nothing, his friend on everything.

She closed the notebook and lay in the dark with the orchestra's tempo still set in her like a metronome, and thought about how the secret had not gotten smaller for having a second keeper. It had gotten staff, a budget, a schedule, a treaty — it had gotten, in every way that mattered, heavier, and the weight was distributed now, and distribution, she was learning, was just another word for more surface to be struck on.
Is a secret safer when two people keep it — or only heavier?

episodes.title: The Donor King
paras: Alumni weekend came down on Bridge Water University the way weather came down on a coast: announced for weeks, undeniable for days, and priced, by the people who worked in it, in loads.

The lettermen came back with their wives and their waistlines and their stories worn smooth as coins, and the building dressed itself for them — banners on the arena's face, the founders' wall polished to a shallow shine — and underneath all of it, in the service corridors where the weekend was actually manufactured, the staff ran the event the way they ran everything: out of carts and crates and a laundry that had not stopped since Tuesday.

Gigi's department had gone into the weekend already owing the building an apology. The extractor — the great steel drum that wrung the wash, the machine the whole laundry's arithmetic stood on — had given its notice in March and been dying, politely and then less politely, ever since. The budget committee had admired the problem twice and deferred it twice, in the grammar committees used for things that happened below stairs: noted, tabled, revisited. In the meantime the towels went through in smaller loads, the uniforms went through twice, and the staff wrung what the machine wouldn't with their hands and their hours, and alumni weekend — four days of commemorations, receptions, an exhibition game, and a donor walkthrough — arrived on top of a laundry that was already three days behind the kingdom's ordinary appetites.

"We get the big man this year," Misty said at the café, in the staff's weather, sliding onto the dryer she was not supposed to sit on with somebody's fries. "Jack himself. Not the checkbook by mail. The whole king, in person, walking the facilities. My supervisor used the word tour like it was a weather event."
"Donors tour," Gigi said, feeding the kingdom's whites into the machine that still worked. "It's what the money does instead of sweating."
"Then let it sweat a little on the extractor," Misty said. "I did the math on a napkin. The napkin's in counseling."

Week twenty arrived on the Tuesday of it, in the middle of the load-in, with no ceremony at all — which was, Gigi thought, counting towels in a corridor while a string quartet rehearsed somewhere above her for a reception she would serve and not attend, exactly the kind of ceremony the whole spring had specialized in.

Twenty. The equator. Half of the arithmetic she had been keeping since December, half of the distance between the championship night and the September the calendar had circled in a hand that was not hers. She stood in the corridor with the count in her head and performed the entry she performed for all the round numbers, which was to price it twice, once in each column. Carried: twenty weeks, alone and then not alone, through a season of other people's announcements. Announced: nothing. The ratio was the spring in one figure, and it was not improving on any schedule she controlled, because the body had begun — politely, in traded shirts and redrawn routes — to file its own announcements, and the body's filing system did not consult her.

The clinic, at least, had become a country she had papers for. The second visit had run the way the first had: her name in clean typeface, the dates confirmed, the bloods back with their numbers in the forgiven ranges, the orchestra measured and pronounced, in the clinician's mild grammar, exactly as expected. Blake's card had paid without ceremony. Blake's car had waited across the street without ceremony. Hope rode home with them again in the May light, uninvited and unbilled, and they were both — this was the treaty's quietest article — learning to let it ride without looking at it directly, the way you let a passenger sleep.

What had changed, in the treaty's second week, was the second clock. It arrived the way all the machine's true announcements arrived below stairs: as a printing job. The print room had run at night for three days — save-the-dates, heavy stock, the kind of card that cost more than Gigi's weekly envelope entire — and Misty, who dealt in information the way she dealt in everything, as a sacrament between broke people, had read the proof over the layout girl's shoulder and carried the text down to the laundry like communion.

"Founders Gala," Misty said. "Late June. Black tie, head table, the whole seating chart at prayer. And printed right on the card, Gavin, in the type they use for weather: at the gala, the families Kreave and Morris will announce the promise." She ate a fry with the concentration of a woman reading fine print. "Announce the announcement. There's a card for the card. The kingdom's efficient, I'll give it that."

Gigi folded the announcement into the arithmetic the way she folded everything, by measurement. Late June. The gala was not new information — the gala had been standing on the calendar since before she had a calendar problem — but the promise's date had been weather, and now it was print, and print had a property weather didn't: it could be counted down to, by anyone, including the girl who would be standing at the staff door of that ballroom in a uniform, at twenty-four weeks, holding a tray.

The secret's deadline, which had run on one clock since February — the body's — acquired a second one that week, and the two clocks did not agree, and she understood, feeding the wash in the steam, that this was the machine's oldest technology: any one deadline could be survived. What ground people down was being counted at from two directions by calendars that had never met.
Jack Kreave arrived on Friday the way his money arrived everywhere: a full hour before he was visible, in arrangements.

The cars came first, and the university's president came down the arena steps in the good suit, and the boosters arranged themselves along the concourse in the formation of men who had been somebody in 1994 and were determined to be informed of it annually. And then the donor-king himself came through the glass doors in the blue May light with Journey at his side like a flag at rest, and the building — Gigi watched it from the tunnel mouth with a cart of commemoratives — did the thing it did for exactly one family: it became, briefly and entirely, a place that was glad to be looked at.

He was good at it. That was the entry she made, fairly, in the column where she kept the things that were true whether she could afford them or not. Jack Kreave did not perform wealth the way the boosters performed it, as nostalgia. He performed it as fluency: he remembered the equipment manager's name from a decade-old banquet and used it; he asked the head trainer about a knee — the trainer's, from the trainer's own playing days — with the recall of a man who kept people the way other men kept portfolios; he shook the hands of two freshmen as though the handshake were a contract he intended to honor. Charm, in Jack Kreave, was not a mood. It was a census, conducted at walking pace, with refreshments.
"That's the hand that wrote the script," Misty said beside her, watching him work the concourse. "Look at it being charming. It's like watching weather be polite."

The exhibition game ran that evening in the dressed arena — the current roster against the returned, the old banners lit — and Blake played the way he had been playing since April, which was to say beautifully and at one remove, the public performance running over an interior nobody in the building could read. Except one. In the tunnel at the quarter break, loading towels with the speed of a girl whose routes had no mirrors left in them, Gigi watched him find the staff door with his eyes for exactly the width of a breath — not a look, the treaty's discipline held; a measurement, the way his hand had stopped on a café counter at a number — and go back out into the light. She priced it in the ledger's new column, the one the treaty had opened: his caution was a form of care now, and care, she was learning, arrived shaped so much like its opposite that only the accounting could tell them apart.

At the alumni bench, in the second quarter, a booster in a letter jacket leaned down the row to Franky with the solicitous expression of a man delivering a diagnosis he had gotten at third hand and was proud of.

"How's the king's knee, son? Word in the building is he's been getting treated. Across town. Off the books." He said it with the warmth of a man offering insurance. "You tell him the alumni look after their own."

Franky laughed with both hands and the whole bench joined him, and the moment passed, and the theory — the wrong fact with the clinic in it, the one Franky himself had carried to the paper's file in an act of loyalty — moved through the returning lettermen like weather through a wheat field, bending everything, breaking nothing, impossible to call back. And in the box above the court, where Jack sat with Journey and the Morrises in the geometry of the announced world, the word reached the donor-king's ear in its third retelling — an aide, a murmur, a courtesy — and Gigi, who was watching the box the way staff watched everything, saw Jack's face do the thing she had never seen it do at a gala or a game: nothing at all, for one second too long. The census had just been handed a figure it had not collected itself. He filed it behind the smile and applauded the play, and the smile stayed, and the filing stayed too.
At halftime the lights went down for the civic presentation, and the arena screen — twenty feet of light above the court, the kingdom's own sky — filled with the city.

It was a clip, ninety seconds, professionally fond: Mayor Klein Calhoun cutting a ribbon downtown, at the new river steps, in the spring sunshine, his name riding under his face in the broadcast's clean typeface, with the council arranged behind him and the avenue's new gates going up in the background like punctuation. The scissors rode in on a cushion. The applause track the arena laid under it was joined, a beat later, by the real thing, rising up out of the seats and into the boxes, where Jack Kreave applauded his friend and peer with the unhurried hands of a man applauding a member of his own government.

episodes.title: Where the Name Gets Washed
paras: Below, at the floor's edge with a crate of towels against her hip, Gigi watched her father's face run twenty feet tall over a basketball court, smiling the smile twenty years of rooms had engraved, while his grandchild — twenty weeks along, unannounced in every record the world kept — rode under a staff shirt in the dark at the margin of the light. She did not count the distance this time. There was no distance to count; a screen had abolished it and made it infinite in the same gesture. She counted the clip instead, the way she counted everything when her heart was busy: ninety seconds, the scissors at forty, the smile held for the lenses at eighty, the whole civic liturgy at the length of a song — and understood, with the clarity the ledger specialized in, that this was what the erasure looked like from the inside at full efficiency. It did not look like cruelty. It looked like applause, in a good suit, at a ribbon, in May. It looked like the whole city agreeing, at the volume of a sporting event, that the man on the screen had no daughter in the building.

The screen went back to basketball. The towels needed the tunnel. She carried them there at furniture speed, and her hands did their job correctly, twice, with her initials available for the count, because that was what hands were for.
The walkthrough came the next morning, in the rinsed light of a building recovering from itself, and it came — as everything real came that spring — disguised as administration.

The athletic director led it, with Castro at his shoulder for the pro-track rooms and the equipment manager carrying the department's hopes in the particular posture of a man who has had a request tabled twice. Jack walked the facilities the way he walked a concourse: completely, at a census-taker's pace, pleased by evidence of order. The training room passed inspection. The weight room earned a story from 1996, told well. And then the route came down, as all routes in that building eventually came down, to the rooms where the kingdom was washed — and the manager, arriving at the laundry's door with the donor-king at his back and the department's whole future riding on his grammar, did the thing managers did: he hedged.
"We're managing, Mr. Kreave," he said, in the voice of a man describing a roof that leaked only when it rained. "The volume's grown with the program, of course. We make it work."

"Managing," Jack repeated, pleasantly, and looked around the steam at the staff running the smaller loads, at the towels going twice through machines that sounded like a household argument, and the pleasantness did the arithmetic out loud: "This room washes two programs' worth of young men, Coach tells me. It doesn't look managed. It looks outnumbered." He turned, in the doorway, to the room at large, with the air of a man asking a question at a table where he was paying for lunch. "What's it actually need?"
The room did what rooms did in the presence of the census: it consulted its shoes.

Gigi answered because the count was her native tongue and the room needed a number more than it needed courage. She gave it the way she gave everything, flat, in staff grammar, with the figures in their order: the extractor, which had carried the building since before the freshmen were born and had filed its resignation in March, in writing, in the form of a bearing that now announced itself two rooms away. The med cabinet's lock, which was a hasp from another century and could be opened by any key the building had ever issued and a few it hadn't. The hours, which the gala calendar would triple in June, against a staff roster that the budget had frozen in February. She priced it the way she priced her own life: by what it cost, what it was for, and what happened if nobody paid. It took forty seconds. When she stopped, the equipment manager was looking at her the way men looked at weather they hadn't ordered, and Jack Kreave was looking at her the way he looked at everything that had ever made him money: with appraisal, complete and entirely unsentimental.
"Name?" he said.
"Gavin, sir. Equipment and laundry."
"Gavin." He said it the way he said everything he intended to keep. "The department runs on Gavin, I take it."
"It runs, sir," she said. "That's the job."

He funded it in the doorway, in front of the staff, with the unceremoniousness of a man signing a lunch check: a figure — named, whole, and larger than the request by exactly the margin that made it a gift instead of a purchase — for the athletics staff fund, extractor first, the lock second, the June hours funded as overtime with his compliments to the people who actually washed the name. The room made the sound rooms made. The manager began a gratitude with both hands. And Jack, raising one finger with the gentleness of a man amending a contract everyone else thought was finished, attached the donor's whole signature in one sentence: "One condition. I walk the rooms once a season, and somebody puts a small plaque by the door, so the young men know the laundry has friends." He smiled at the room. "Generosity should have a name on it. Otherwise it's just weather."

So the machine fed her department in her doorway, in May, with her initials due on the paperwork by Monday: the invoice, the acknowledgment, the thank-you that the fund's procedures required, in her small clean hand, thanking Jack Kreave for the machines that washed his family's name. She smiled the smile her job had issued her and took the details down correctly, twice, and understood — standing in the steam with the figures still warm — that the generosity and the occupation were the same gesture, and always had been: his money now ran her rooms, his walkthroughs would now enter them on a schedule, his name would now hang by her door in small brass letters, and every part of it was a kindness the department genuinely needed and she genuinely could not refuse. That was the technology. Refusable gifts were just purchases. His were load-bearing.

"Show me where the name gets washed," he said, when the paperwork had a home, and so the staff ghost gave the donor-king the tour: the sorters with their bins by program, the tape wall where a hundred names waited in line for the wash — KREAVE at the head of the alphabet's privileges and the roster's alike, a row of the family's surname stitched and stacked like a small standing army — the machines, the steam, the whole below-stairs kingdom of which she was, for forty minutes, the crowned and only guide. He was charming throughout, in the census way: he asked how the names were kept from migrating between programs, and she told him; he asked whether the staff ate, and the manager answered too quickly; he touched, once, the name tape on a practice jersey with the absent attention of a man reading a document in a language he owned.
"You know every name in this room," he said at the end, at the door, almost idly.
"That's the job, sir."

"Most people above stairs couldn't name three of the hands that dress them." He looked at her once more, completely, in the appraisal register — and somewhere in the look, at a depth the room couldn't read, there was the smallest item filed and left: recognition's envelope, unopened, addressed to a face seen somewhere, leaving somewhere, at a gala in the spring. He did not open it. Donor-kings did not open envelopes in laundry rooms. "Bridge Water's lucky to have staff who count," he said, and the tour moved on into the light, and the door sighed behind it, and Gigi stood in the steam with her hands in the kingdom's towels and priced what it cost to be appraised as furniture by the machine's author and found excellent.
Blake found her at load-out, in the hour when the building belonged to the staff, with his bag over his shoulder and the exhibition's tape still on his wrists.

"He asked the manager about you after," he said. "By name. Wanted to know how long Gavin had run the department." A breath. "And at the reception he told my mother the help's loyal this year. In front of the Morrises. Like a compliment to the building."

"His walkthroughs come with the money," Gigi said. "Seasonal. Announced. He'll be in my rooms four times a year with a clipboard of goodwill, Blake. Your father is installing himself in the laundry like a plaque."

"I saw him look at you in the doorway. When you gave him the numbers." Blake's voice stayed down, in the treaty register, and she could hear the arithmetic running under it like a second pulse. "And I looked at you when he did it. He saw that too. On the concourse, first hour — he watched me watch the tunnel door. He didn't say anything. He filed it under my character. Kings know the staff, he told Franky. Good management." He shook his head, once, with the exhausted precision of a man reading his own file. "My father's charm is a census, Gigi. He came down here to count the building and now the count has your name in it, spelled the way I say it in my head."

"Then we give the census nothing to add," she said. "The treaty holds. You don't look, I don't stand where the looking lands, and your father funds my extractor and hangs his name by my door and believes, at full price, that he has purchased a loyal department." She set the last stack down in its order. "It's the best camouflage anyone ever bought me, Blake. He paid for it himself."

That night she did the books in the dorm with Pest asleep in the top bunk and the summer coming on through the window screen, and counted the envelope with hands that smelled of the building's soap: two hundred and sixty-three dollars. Two hundred and forty, and twenty-three more from the alumni weekend — boosters tipping like the century owed an apology, reunion classes buying coffee for the staff ghosts who had carried their towels in another life. His father's envelope stood in her locker across the building, unopened, acquiring a neighbor: a brass plaque, on order, with the donor's name for her doorway.
She wrote the week's number in the margin — 20, small and clean — and underneath it, in the second column, the entry for the era the machine had just inaugurated:
Fed: my machines, by his hand. Smiled: on the invoice. Owed: a plaque, and four walkthroughs a year. Clocks: two now. Both his.

She closed the notebook and lay in the dark with the orchestra keeping its own hours under her hand and thought about a sentence printed on heavy stock in a print room at night, and a face twenty feet tall applauded by a box full of fathers, and how the machine had looked at the very hands that were hurting it, appraised them, and fed them — all in one weekend, all with perfect manners.
When the machine feeds the very hands that are hurting it, is that generosity — or camouflage it bought by accident?

episodes.title: The Fall
paras: Erin kept her landing gear in a blue pouch with her name taped to it in two places, the way people labeled things they could not afford to lose.

That was what the squad called it — her landing gear — the prescribed tablets she took before practice to steady what needed steadying: hands, nerves, the fine inner machinery a flyer depended on at the top of a stunt, three bodies high, where the air had opinions. She took them at the med cabinet with the ceremony of a girl performing a sacrament in public: the pouch unzipped, the tablet counted onto her palm, the water swallowed in one practiced motion, and then the transformation the whole squad traded on — Erin, ordinary Erin, butter-fingered Erin of the warm-up drills, assembling herself into the stillest person in the building.

"Say it," Steff said that Tuesday, watching the ritual from the bench with a captain's proprietary pride, while the spring floor filled with mats and the gala showcase routine took its shape in chalk marks and arguments. "Say the thing."

"Steady hands," Erin said, grinning, wiggling her fingers like a pianist showing off, "steady nerves, no funerals." She zipped the pouch with a flourish. "My mother is coming to the gala, you know. First time she'll ever see me fly. Twenty-one years she's driven me to gyms, and Bridge Water finally gives her a ballroom to watch it in." She said it to the room, to the mats, to nobody's custody in particular, and then she went out onto the floor and began, as she began every practice, by being caught.

Gigi heard all of it from the med room doorway with a count in her hands, which was where she heard everything, and the hearing went into the ledger in the column that had no heading: a face, a mother, a ballroom. She had been doing the books on the gala showcase for a week by then, since the print room's night shift had given the promise a date. The showcase was the gala's jewel — the squad's finale, three minutes of flight in evening light, Layna radiant at the center of it and Erin at the top of the final pyramid, the photograph of the night: the approved girl crowned in bodies, the announcement's halo made of girls. The arithmetic Gigi had written in the margin, in the audit she now performed on every rung before she climbed it, ran clean and small and entirely deniable. Aim: a shaken flyer. Erin rattled at a Tuesday practice — hands unreliable, a stunt pulled down early by a careful coach, the showcase's finale simplified in a panic of re-choreography, the halo dimmed to something the announcement's photographs would have to work around. Price: one swap, from the cabinet she stocked, of tablets that lived two shelves apart in identical institutional amber. She aimed, as she had aimed in March, at a message and a benching. The margin said so, in her small clean hand, in ink.
